item.title: Critical launch for Vulcan as ULA targets Friday the 13th
item.description: United Launch Alliance (ULA) has set a target date for its return to flight: Friday, November 13, for a Vulcan launch. The mission will send 40 Amazon Leo satellites into orbit. A pair of BE-4 engines will power the booster, along with six Solid Rocket Boosters (SRBs). A Centaur V second stage, propelled by two RL10C-1 engines, will complete the journey to orbit and deploy the payload. The launch is the first Vulcan launch for Amazon after eight deployments with ULA's Atlas V. It is also the first since the launch earlier this year for the US Space Force in which an SRB burned through its nozzle during the ascent, treating viewers to some impressive fireworks and controllers to some likely clenched sphincters thanks to a "significant performance anomaly." In the event, the US Space Force payload successfully reached orbit, but the Vulcan was stood down while ULA conducted an investigation. This wasn't the first time a Vulcan had had issues with its SRBs. A nozzle was shed during the second launch of the rocket in 2024. Things went OK with the third launch. But another problem on the fourth trek to orbit meant a stand-down was unavoidable. The workhorse Atlas V has continued deploying Amazon Leo satellites during the Vulcan's hiatus. Another 29 were added on a July 2 launch from Space Launch Complex-41 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force station. However, Amazon booked 38 Vulcan rocket launches – quite an increase from the eight Atlas V launches ULA has already performed for Leo. It is obviously keen to add more satellites to its growing constellation. The SRBs are Northrop Grumman units, and the six Graphite Epoxy Motor (GEM) 63XL units will each provide an additional 459,600 lbs (2,044 kN) of thrust at liftoff. That's assuming nothing unexpected burns through or falls off. ULA has not detailed the results of its investigation or any changes it had to make. ULA said: "The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the solid rocket booster (SRB) anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle. To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission. By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers." US Space Force and Amazon are ULA's biggest customers - and Space Force will be watching. ULA came second to SpaceX in contracts awarded by Space Force for FY25 to FY29 . ®

item.title: SpaceX fires up Starship upper stage ahead of landmark Flight 15 test launch (video)
item.description: null SpaceX just checked another big box on the path to its 15th Starship test flight, which promises to be pretty epic. The company conducted static-fire tests with Starship 's Ship upper stage on Monday (Oct. 26) and Tuesday (Oct. 27), igniting its Raptor engines while the vehicle, known as Ship 42, remained anchored to the ground. "Ship 42 static fires complete. The Starship preparing for Flight 15 performed a full duration, six-engine static fire, and fired a single Raptor engine to simulate a deorbit burn," SpaceX said in a Wednesday (Oct. 28) X post that shared video of the tests. SpaceX conducts a six-engine static fire test with its Flight 15 Starship upper stage on Oct. 27, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) The Ship 42 tests come on the heels of a successful 33-engine static fire with Booster 22 , the Starship Super Heavy first stage that will conduct Flight 15. Everything therefore appears to remain on track for Flight 15, which SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has said is targeted for sometime in November. All Starship launches are worth watching, but this one should be particularly exciting. Musk said last week that SpaceX will try to catch both Ship and Super Heavy during Flight 15, provided the company can get regulatory approval to do so. These catches are performed by the "chopstick" arms of the launch tower at Starbase, SpaceX's Starship launch and manufacturing hub in South Texas. The company has snagged Super Heavy on three Starship test flights to date but has not yet attempted a Ship capture. Double chopstick catches will be the norm on operational Starship launches, if all goes to plan. This recovery strategy will reduce the time needed to get Super Heavy and Ship ready for reflight, significantly boosting launch cadences, according to SpaceX. (Starship is designed to be fully reusable, unlike SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets, whose upper stages are expendable.) SpaceX is already riding a historic success with Starship: The megarocket reached orbit for the first time ever on Flight 14 , which took place on Sept. 28. And Ship deployed 26 of the company's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites during that flight, starting the assembly of a new broadband constellation that Musk has said will eventually consist of 100,000 spacecraft . Starlink V3 missions will therefore make up a significant percentage of Starship launches for the foreseeable future. But SpaceX also plans to use the megarocket to build an even bigger constellation in Earth orbit — Starmind , which could harbor one million of the company's AI data center satellites.

item.title: Massive leak exposes 41,000 DHS workers and undercover ICE agents
item.description: An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates. The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” Read full article Comments

item.title: Shortlist of age checks for the UK's under-16 social media ban is out, 'some' adults will need verifying
item.description: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban. The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process. Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online." Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year. The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today. The methods put forward include: Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check. The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered. Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services. item.dc:creator: Connor Jones
item.content:encoded: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban. The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process. Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online." Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year. The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today. The methods put forward include: Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check. The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered. Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services. It estimates that around 94 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a form of photo ID, such as a passport, driving licence, or an ID card certified by the Proof of Age Standards Scheme, and that around 150,000 have neither. BBW's Carlo added: "Hundreds of thousands of people without ID, who tend to be poorer people, and many more who don’t want to risk handing their passports over to foreign tech companies will be locked out of huge parts of the internet. "The plan will kill anonymity online, whilst the UK’s culture of speech policing is reaching a crisis point. The policy is painfully misguided, an Orwellian assault on free speech and privacy, and will make children no safer at all." 'Circumvention inevitable' Ofcom admitted that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated," as some children will find ways to bypass these age checks, no matter how fully they are implemented. It cited Australia sporadically in its announcement, a country that introduced an under-16 social media ban in December 2025, but has struggled with a large proportion of children devising ways to circumvent these checks. Ofcom said the UK government intends to adopt, but learn lessons from, Australia’s rollout, committing to implementing more robust measures that promote the ban’s aims. It said it has identified some mitigations that could be taken to counter circumvention, such as making it easier for users to report suspected underage social media users, and “using age inference models.” The regulator said it will closely monitor circumvention for the first 12 months after the ban is enforced to understand possible methods to prevent children from finding ways around the age checks. In May, nearly a year after the OSA’s age verification requirements kicked in, researchers found that the existing age checks proved largely ineffective at keeping under-18s away from adult content online. Some reported beating age checks with just a drawn-on moustache . England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, said recently that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children’s ability to access potentially harmful online content. Commenting on today’s announcement , Ofcom chief exec Dame Melanie Dawes said that when the social media ban takes effect, it will take a whole-of-society approach to ensure the ban is upheld. ?This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right," she said. "It can work if social media firms do highly effective age checks properly, and we’ve set out ways that could be achieved. When it comes into force next year, we’ll be ready to take swift and firm action against any company that fails to comply. "We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk. This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play." The UK government is expected to outline the first set of regulations related to the under-16 social media ban by the end of the year, and Ofcom is in the process of developing draft guidance for platforms. ®

item.title: Attackers turn GitHub issues into supply chain campaign against 61 public repos in less than an hour
item.description: EXCLUSIVE Researchers identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories, including popular open source projects such as Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave browser, and MLflow, in what they suspect is a coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens. It all happened very quickly, the Radware threat hunters said in an exclusive interview with The Register . Most (77) of the malicious items were published during a 43-minute time span on September 1, with the remaining six occurring within the next two minutes. “Our guess is that the final aim was a supply-chain attack in which the attacker gains credentials for the repo, and then he has the power to change the contents – the code – as he wishes” and then push the malicious changes to others, Radware VP and researcher Gabi Nakibly told The Register . Nakibly and fellow Radware researcher Zvika Babo say they suspect a single individual is behind this supply chain campaign. This attacker used 74 different GitHub accounts, many of which had legitimate development histories, meaning they were likely compromised. "Considering that dozens of accounts posted the same type of payload, on the same day, within a narrow time window, and to the same infrastructure, it is reasonable to assess that the activity was coordinated,” the team wrote in research shared ahead of publication with The Register . A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain campaign novel, and extremely stealthy. First, the attacker publishes an issue, pull request, or comment containing malicious commands hidden in HTML comments. This ensures the content is not visible in the rendered page. Plus, a GitHub event – like a pull request or issue – can automatically trigger a workflow if the repository is configured to respond to that event, meaning the attacker can be pretty hands-off at this point. “The workflow automatically is triggered within a second, and if the workflow is indeed vulnerable, then the attack is executed successfully,” Nakibly said. The workflow incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code, and the shell executes the hidden, malicious command, which hoovers up environment variables and attempts to exfiltrate those to an attacker-controlled server. While the researchers examined logs from actual runs, and told us they found two cases containing evidence that the malicious command ran inside the automation environment, they can’t definitively say whether the attacker successfully obtained repository write permissions, modified source code, or compromised downstream software. But they're trying. “The big picture is that the attackers are trying to find every possible way to get inside the repos to get credentials,” Nakibly said. item.content:encoded: EXCLUSIVE Researchers identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories, including popular open source projects such as Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave browser, and MLflow, in what they suspect is a coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens. It all happened very quickly, the Radware threat hunters said in an exclusive interview with The Register . Most (77) of the malicious items were published during a 43-minute time span on September 1, with the remaining six occurring within the next two minutes. “Our guess is that the final aim was a supply-chain attack in which the attacker gains credentials for the repo, and then he has the power to change the contents – the code – as he wishes” and then push the malicious changes to others, Radware VP and researcher Gabi Nakibly told The Register . Nakibly and fellow Radware researcher Zvika Babo say they suspect a single individual is behind this supply chain campaign. This attacker used 74 different GitHub accounts, many of which had legitimate development histories, meaning they were likely compromised. "Considering that dozens of accounts posted the same type of payload, on the same day, within a narrow time window, and to the same infrastructure, it is reasonable to assess that the activity was coordinated,” the team wrote in research shared ahead of publication with The Register . A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain campaign novel, and extremely stealthy. First, the attacker publishes an issue, pull request, or comment containing malicious commands hidden in HTML comments. This ensures the content is not visible in the rendered page. Plus, a GitHub event – like a pull request or issue – can automatically trigger a workflow if the repository is configured to respond to that event, meaning the attacker can be pretty hands-off at this point. “The workflow automatically is triggered within a second, and if the workflow is indeed vulnerable, then the attack is executed successfully,” Nakibly said. The workflow incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code, and the shell executes the hidden, malicious command, which hoovers up environment variables and attempts to exfiltrate those to an attacker-controlled server. While the researchers examined logs from actual runs, and told us they found two cases containing evidence that the malicious command ran inside the automation environment, they can’t definitively say whether the attacker successfully obtained repository write permissions, modified source code, or compromised downstream software. But they're trying. “The big picture is that the attackers are trying to find every possible way to get inside the repos to get credentials,” Nakibly said. Plus, “the attacker doesn't need to compromise the repository or to have access to its codebase” to do this, Babo added. “Basically, every user with a GitHub account can try to run this attack – it's very easy to start this attack.” Which repos were affected? As of October 13, the threat hunters identified 83 GitHub items with a verified payload across 61 different repositories. The repos span AI frameworks, security tools, development infrastructure, databases, and other widely used open source software projects. The Radware report lists agno-agi/agno (42.7K stars), ToolJet/ToolJet (41.1K), google/langextract (38.9K), aquasecurity/trivy (38.4K), CopilotKit/CopilotKit (38K), and podman-container-tools/podman (33K), among the most popular. Other notable targets included QwenLM/qwen-code (28.5K), mlflow/mlflow (28.4K), discordjs/discord.js (26.8K), cilium/cilium (25.6K), brave/brave-browser (23.9K), dotnet/maui (23.3K), Homebrew/homebrew-cask (22.2K), github/docs (21K), apache/doris (16K), and PX4/PX4-Autopilot (12.8K). “These projects are used by thousands of organizations," Babo said. The researchers disclosed their findings to all of the projects’ maintainers, and most of the repositories were closed or fixed, but they can’t confirm that all of them were. This campaign follows several earlier supply chain attacks against open source security and dev tools as attackers increasingly look for new methods to steal credentials and other secrets . “There is no way to stop the attackers from attempting,” Nakibly said. “The only way is to make sure that the workflow code is resilient, and not vulnerable to such attacks." The researchers recommend applying least-privilege access to CI/CD workflows, and separating as much as possible workflows triggered by external events from jobs with elevated permissions. “Developers should treat external content as untrusted, and also limit the secrets and environment variables that are available to the workflow,” Babo said. ®

item.title: Stunning solar eclipse photos reveal giant hole and mysterious 'smoke rings' in the sun's atmosphere
item.description:
Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. Originally from Prague, the Czech Republic, she spent the first seven years of her career working as a reporter, script-writer and presenter for various TV programmes of the Czech Public Service Television. She later took a career break to pursue further education and added a Master's in Science from the International Space University, France, to her Bachelor's in Journalism and Master's in Cultural Anthropology from Prague's Charles University. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

Newly released photographs of the sun captured during the Aug. 12 total solar eclipse reveal the sun's outer atmosphere in unprecedented detail. The images, released by researchers working as part of the Solar Wind Sherpas project coordinated by the University of Hawaii, also show rare structures in the solar wind known as smoke rings. Named for their resemblance to the circles blown by smokers, these vortices were first identified in solar eclipse photographs captured in 2008. The researchers had long struggled to explain the processes behind their formation. They now know the rings are a result of the temperature differences in the coronal plasma and spread along the sun 's magnetic lines deep into interplanetary space. "This year, we have managed to capture those smoke rings really well," Miloslav Druckmüller, a professor of mathematics at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic, who leads the image processing efforts for the Solar Wind Sherpas Team, said in a statement . "They are beautifully twisted vortices and there are very many of them in the corona." The images, taken from the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, also reveal a giant coronal hole — an opening in the sun's magnetic field lines — through which solar wind can escape more readily at very high speeds of up to 500 miles per second (800 kilometers per second). Coronal holes are cooler regions in the sun's atmosphere that appear darker in extreme ultraviolet and X-ray images taken by probes in space. They form in regions where the sun's magnetic field lines extend outward into space rather than looping back to the surface, allowing high-speed solar wind to escape. These structures can persist for weeks or even months. High-res images of the sun taken during the total solar eclipse of August 2026 reveal a coronal hole and intriguing structures known as smoke rings in the solar corona. Click the right arrow for an annotated version. Brno University of Technology/Miloslav Druckmüller Annotated high-res images of the sun taken during the total solar eclipse of August 2026 reveal a coronal hole and intriguing structures known as smoke rings in the sola

She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

Named for their resemblance to the circles blown by smokers, these vortices were first identified in solar eclipse photographs captured in 2008. The researchers had long struggled to explain the processes behind their formation. They now know the rings are a result of the temperature differences in the coronal plasma and spread along the sun 's magnetic lines deep into interplanetary space. "This year, we have managed to capture those smoke rings really well," Miloslav Druckmüller, a professor of mathematics at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic, who leads the image processing efforts for the Solar Wind Sherpas Team, said in a statement . "They are beautifully twisted vortices and there are very many of them in the corona." The images, taken from the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, also reveal a giant coronal hole — an opening in the sun's magnetic field lines — through which solar wind can escape more readily at very high speeds of up to 500 miles per second (800 kilometers per second). Coronal holes are cooler regions in the sun's atmosphere that appear darker in extreme ultraviolet and X-ray images taken by probes in space. They form in regions where the sun's magnetic field lines extend outward into space rather than looping back to the surface, allowing high-speed solar wind to escape. These structures can persist for weeks or even months. High-res images of the sun taken during the total solar eclipse of August 2026 reveal a coronal hole and intriguing structures known as smoke rings in the solar corona. Click the right arrow for an annotated version. Brno University of Technology/Miloslav Druckmüller Annotated high-res images of the sun taken during the total solar eclipse of August 2026 reveal a coronal hole and intriguing structures known as smoke rings in the solar corona. Brno University of Technology/Miloslav Druckmüller Solar eclipse photography provides a unique vista into the processes taking place in the sun's upper atmosphere, the corona, which remain hidden even to cutting-edge space-based observatories. Space probes and astronomical telescopes on Earth rely on instruments known as coronagraphs to view the corona. As the corona is a million times dimmer than the sun's surface, researchers need to obscure the visible solar disk with an occulter to view it. This occulter, located inside the telescope, has to cover a larger area than just the solar disk itself to protect the images from the effects of diffraction. During a total solar eclipse , the moon naturally blocks the sun's bright disk, allowing scientists to capture exceptionally detailed views of the inner corona that are difficult to obtain with conventional coronographs.

item.title: LibreOffice's 'no AI' stance meets LLM-assisted code
item.description: The Document Foundation (TDF) says LibreOffice has no built-in AI features and that its core developers do not use LLMs - but community contributors face different rules. In a Fediverse post , someone who goes by the handle of argv[-1] highlights three LibreOffice commits this year that acknowledge the use of LLM coding assistants. Two of them – Inheritance when setting paragraph style font size to 100% or +0pt and Enable relative font sizes in Calc cell styles – date from April and credit Claude with helping identify the fixes. More recently, September's Add Copy Image button to screenshot dialog acknowledges using GitHub Copilot in VS Code to generate the BitmapTransferable class, while the copyButtonHandler method was written manually with LLM/code-completion assistance. This is hardly a fatal flaw – after all, it's getting hard to find any major FOSS project with absolutely no LLM-generated code in it these days. However, The Document Foundation says that the leading FOSS office suite is AI-free. As we noted when it released version 26.8 in August , we interpret this statement as a jab at its former development partner Collabora. Back in June, we noted that increased AI integration was a headline feature in Collabora CODE 26.04 . CODE is Collabora's web-based office suite, based on LibreOffice code. TDF – the primary maintainer and custodian of LibreOffice since its 2010 fork from Oracle-controlled OpenOffice.org – has made the absence of built-in AI a selling point. In September, it published a blog post declaring that no AI is now a feature . Meanwhile, on October 21, TDF announced 9.4 million downloads over eight weeks – excluding Windows updates and downloads of older releases, which are counted separately. The foundation acknowledged that the reasons for the growth are difficult to determine. TDF's direct response on Mastodon is dismissive: "Ah, another high-quality Mastodon discussion. Again: No core developers use LLMs. We rely on contributions from the wider community and don't explicitly list tools people can't use – but we do require people disclose when they use LLMs and generally discourage the practice. We carefully review submissions by contributors to make sure the code quality is good and that the patch author understands their own code. LLMs are prohibited for students. That is not 'slop'." In other words, TDF's approach resembles what some commenters have compared to the Debian approach : LLM coding assistants are permitted for some contributors, subject to disclosure and human review. For AI advocates, this is the only pragmatic response – which could be summarized as the "AI is just a tool" school of thought. However, since this admission does seem to contradict the very visible public no-AI message, some LibreOffice users are really rather unhappy. Our favorite comment so far is from Argentinian developer Federico Schonborn , who slyly noted : "When a bakery announces they won't put asbestos in their cake frosting you mus

More recently, September's Add Copy Image button to screenshot dialog acknowledges using GitHub Copilot in VS Code to generate the BitmapTransferable class, while the copyButtonHandler method was written manually with LLM/code-completion assistance. This is hardly a fatal flaw – after all, it's getting hard to find any major FOSS project with absolutely no LLM-generated code in it these days. However, The Document Foundation says that the leading FOSS office suite is AI-free. As we noted when it released version 26.8 in August , we interpret this statement as a jab at its former development partner Collabora. Back in June, we noted that increased AI integration was a headline feature in Collabora CODE 26.04 . CODE is Collabora's web-based office suite, based on LibreOffice code. TDF – the primary maintainer and custodian of LibreOffice since its 2010 fork from Oracle-controlled OpenOffice.org – has made the absence of built-in AI a selling point. In September, it published a blog post declaring that no AI is now a feature . Meanwhile, on October 21, TDF announced 9.4 million downloads over eight weeks – excluding Windows updates and downloads of older releases, which are counted separately. The foundation acknowledged that the reasons for the growth are difficult to determine. TDF's direct response on Mastodon is dismissive: "Ah, another high-quality Mastodon discussion. Again: No core developers use LLMs. We rely on contributions from the wider community and don't explicitly list tools people can't use – but we do require people disclose when they use LLMs and generally discourage the practice. We carefully review submissions by contributors to make sure the code quality is good and that the patch author understands their own code. LLMs are prohibited for students. That is not 'slop'." In other words, TDF's approach resembles what some commenters have compared to the Debian approach : LLM coding assistants are permitted for some contributors, subject to disclosure and human review. For AI advocates, this is the only pragmatic response – which could be summarized as the "AI is just a tool" school of thought. However, since this admission does seem to contradict the very visible public no-AI message, some LibreOffice users are really rather unhappy. Our favorite comment so far is from Argentinian developer Federico Schonborn , who slyly noted : "When a bakery announces they won't put asbestos in their cake frosting you must not point out they're already putting asbestos in their cake filling, you see." We asked TDF’s spokesman Italo Vignoli for comment. He pointed us to TDF's Development/AI policy , and added: "There isn't any departure from the public statements about LO 26.8, as they were about user features and not about development." As "Skjeggtroll" succinctly put it : "It strikes me as odd to ban all use of LLM for the commit message , but still allow its use for the actual code." ®

item.title: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip
item.description: Liquid Static Studio; PC You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing There was always something creepy about the job-simulator genre. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop. Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets. Once on the plane, you roll your trolley down the aisle, serving booze and inedible meals, and occasionally dealing with passenger complaints. Then the plane crashes and, frankly, it all goes downhill from there. Continue reading...

item.title: SpaceX no longer needs NASA, and that's a problem for America's space agency
item.description: For nearly a quarter of a century, Elon Musk and his essential partner at SpaceX, Gwynne Shotwell, viewed the United States government as El Dorado, the mythical city of gold. Like machete-wielding treasure hunters, Musk and Shotwell hacked through a tangled jungle filled with lurking carnivores such as Boeing and Lockheed Martin, as well as bean counters and regulators. Over time, against long odds, the pair cleared a path for SpaceX to contracts at NASA and the US military. They sued when things did not go their way. They hollered about unfair playing fields. Most importantly, they delivered quality space products to the US government for less. And so, after a while, SpaceX found El Dorado and a city of contracts. Read full article Comments

item.title: Traces of new Pi hardware spotted in GitHub
item.description: The wait for a new Raspberry Pi Zero may be nearly over, judging by the raspberrypi/linux repository. Among the merged pull requests is one titled "Add device tree for Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4A," suggesting new hardware is on the way, including a successor to the very long-in-the-tooth Pi Zero 2 W. The board launched five years ago. Its 512 MB of memory was hardly generous, but it offered considerable bang for the buck. At the time, we reckoned performance was closer to the Raspberry Pi 3 than the flagship Pi 4, but perfectly adequate provided you didn't open too many browser tabs at once. According to the source tree, as reported by Phoronix , the new board could use the Broadcom BCM271, up from the RP3A0 in the current Zero. If so, that would be a significant performance gain, though it's unclear whether the 1.5GHz clock speed of the Pi 4, which uses the same SoC, will be retained. Heat is a concern as the Pi 4 gained a reputation for running hot under load without active cooling, and it throttles performance when temperatures climb. A board as small as the Zero will have even less room to shed heat. Assuming that challenge can be met, it would be a worthy upgrade for the venerable Pi Zero 2. There is no word on how much memory it is likely to have – we can't imagine much given the current cost of RAM and the need to keep the price at least close to that of the Zero 2 W, which can still be had for around $18. The code also hints at eMMC storage is mentioned, but that seems unlikely to reach the finished product, probably because of the cost. Alongside the Pi Zero 3 W is a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A. Where the Zero 3 W is a clear upgrade, the 4 Model A looks more like a cost-cutting measure amid rising hardware prices. Model A boards typically have less memory, and no Ethernet port, and the 4A appears to have a single HDMI output rather than two. Things could change before any hardware ships. We asked Raspberry Pi if anything was in the pipeline, but the company said it had nothing to add. Enthusiasts will welcome an upgraded Pi Zero after more than half a decade, provided the price is right and it doesn't run too hot. At the same time, a cut-down Pi 4 carries the whiff of inevitability in an era of rising component costs. ®

item.title: Microsoft breaks New Outlook attachment opening with Edge Update
item.description: Users of New Outlook wondering where the option to open an attachment went have a culprit to blame – an Edge update. The issue underscores how interconnected things are in the Microsoft ecosystem. According to the vendor, an update to Edge 156 "unintentionally enabled an unnecessary configuration," which means some New Outlook users are unable to open email file attachments. An error stating the file cannot be opened also appears for some, along with an instruction to restart Outlook. However, the "Open" option goes away after the error is encountered. A workaround is to use "Save As" to save the attachment, and then open the file manually. Microsoft confirmed the issue yesterday afternoon in the advisory EX1528992, and early this morning began rolling out a fix to disable the "unnecessary" configuration. It expects that it'll take 12 hours for the fix to be rolled out, and users will have to close and reopen New Outlook to feel the benefit. The problem raises some interesting questions. While we'd understand how something unexpected in Edge might cause rendering issues in New Outlook, losing the ability to open attachments because of something an Edge update did is concerning and may make some administrators reconsider the blast radius of software updates. We asked Microsoft for more information about the "unnecessary configuration" and will update this piece should it respond. However, the incident highlights connections within Windows that might surprise users. In addition, it shows that, despite a woeful showing on the desktop market share front – although Edge recently "surged" to almost 15 percent last month, according to Statcounter, up from around 10 percent for much of the year – Microsoft's browser can still capture user attention. It's just not the sort of attention the Windows maker might have hoped for. It is also worth noting that Outlook Classic does not appear to be affected by the issue (according to Microsoft's EX1528992 advisory for Exchange Online). Impacted users could therefore temporarily add opening attachments to the list of things the old software does that the new software doesn't. ®

item.title: Despite the teething issues, Dyson’s Camerajet toothbrush packs in a lot of clever tech – but is it worth £420?
item.description: Dyson’s first electric toothbrush watches you brush and flosses for you, but there are far cheaper ways to get an effective clean • The best electric toothbrushes for every budget When Dyson announced it was entering the toothbrush market , the world responded almost as one: “Four hundred and twenty pounds? For a toothbrush!?” No, it wasn’t a stray decimal point – or if it was, Dyson is doubling down and leaning into the mistake. Unlike high-end brushes from Oral-B or Philips Sonicare, where the “recommended” in “recommended retail price” is doing a heroic amount of heavy lifting given the frequent discounts, the Dyson CameraJet will actually set you back £419.99. Continue reading...

item.title: SpaceX's Starfall capsule delivers cargo for US Air Force in landmark 'point to point' space mission
item.description: null The U.S. Air Force is opening up about the SpaceX Starfall cargo capsule it flew on a recent rideshare mission to orbit — and showing off what the capsule carried. The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) completed a point-to-point rocket cargo delivery test using the secretive uncrewed reentry vehicle, confirming on social media its recovery of the package in the Pacific Ocean. "With support from SpaceX , the AFRL agile cargo pods were recovered after splashdown," the AFRL wrote in an X post on Oct. 26. The Starfall capsule launched on a Falcon 9 rocket as a part of SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 mission, which lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 20 . Starfall carried a number of AFRL-developed cargo pods designed to transport military equipment through space and back to Earth . The successful recovery of the pods marks a big step forward in the Air Force's effort to examine the viability of point-to-point (P2D) rocket cargo missions. "This was a critical achievement to demonstrate the potential of Rocket Cargo delivery for point-to-point rapid global mobility for the Future Force," said AFRL Technology Transition Office director Adam Remaly in a press release on Oct. 20. Photos included in the AFRL social media post show military personnel unpacking a recovered cargo pod for inspection. Each pod contained sensors to monitor temperature conditions through launch, reentry and splashdown, as well as to measure the shock and vibration forces exerted on its cargo. For its first Starfall mission, AFRL packed its cargo pods with representative items like medical equipment, food ration packs and other military kit that might be helpful for surviving an emergency somewhere that's tough to reach via conventional transportation. To that end, AFRL said it also conducted a fit check of a UNI-PAC III life raft inside Starfall, which could potentially be included in future tests. With support from SpaceX, the AFRL agile cargo pods were recovered after splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. AFRL Each pod contained representative mission equipment to study the effects of temperature, shock, and vibration of the cargo environments during launch and reentry. AFRL With support from @SpaceX, the AFRL agile cargo pods were recovered after splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. Each pod contained representative mission equipment to study the effects of temperature, shock, and vibration of the cargo environments during launch and reentry. #Readiness https://t.co/yWoND13ur4 October 26, 2026 "Researchers paid special attention to the electronics equipment and survival gear, including a SATCOM-enabled tracker, batteries, a reverse osmosis desalinator, survival gear and emergency medical equipment," AFRL said in its release. The Starfall capsule launched on a Falcon 9 rocket as a part of SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 mission, which lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 20 . Starfall carried a number of AFRL-developed cargo pods designed to transport military equipment through space and back to Earth . The successful recovery of the pods marks a big step forward in the Air Force's effort to examine the viability of point-to-point (P2D) rocket cargo missions. "This was a critical achievement to demonstrate the potential of Rocket Cargo delivery for point-to-point rapid global mobility for the Future Force," said AFRL Technology Transition Office director Adam Remaly in a press release on Oct. 20. Photos included in the AFRL social media post show military personnel unpacking a recovered cargo pod for inspection. Each pod contained sensors to monitor temperature conditions through launch, reentry and splashdown, as well as to measure the shock and vibration forces exerted on its cargo. For its first Starfall mission, AFRL packed its cargo pods with representative items like medical equipment, food ration packs and other military kit that might be helpful for surviving an emergency somewhere that's tough to reach via conventional transportation. To that end, AFRL said it also conducted a fit check of a UNI-PAC III life raft inside Starfall, which could potentially be included in future tests. With support from SpaceX, the AFRL agile cargo pods were recovered after splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. AFRL Each pod contained representative mission equipment to study the effects of temperature, shock, and vibration of the cargo environments during launch and reentry. AFRL With support from @SpaceX, the AFRL agile cargo pods were recovered after splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. Each pod contained representative mission equipment to study the effects of temperature, shock, and vibration of the cargo environments during launch and reentry. #Readiness https://t.co/yWoND13ur4 October 26, 2026 "Researchers paid special attention to the electronics equipment and survival gear, including a SATCOM-enabled tracker, batteries, a reverse osmosis desalinator, survival gear and emergency medical equipment," AFRL said in its release. SpaceX's disk-shaped Starfall capsule made a quiet debut on a Falcon 9 launch in June, and the company has remained relatively quiet about the vehicle to date. Most of what we do know comes from a Federal Aviation Administration environmental assessment published earlier this year. Starfall measures about 3.1 meters across. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Artist rendering of Starfall entering the atmosphere. SpaceX The hockey-puck-looking vehicle measures approximately 10.2 feet (3.1 meters) across and can return up to 2,200 pounds (1,000 kilograms) of cargo from orbit, according to that report. And it sports a carbon fiber heat shield and compressed gas thrusters for attitude control during reentry, as well as a parachute system for precision landings. AFRL will assess the data recovered from the Oct. 20 mission to contribute to its broader Rocket Cargo initiative, which the Air Force hopes can evolve to the transportation of tens of tons of cargo per launch. That would exceed Starfall's mass capacity, but Starfall isn't the only vehicle the military has considered for its Rocket Cargo program. SpaceX's much larger Starship rocket, which is still under development, was a likely candidate for tests at Johnston Atoll , a remote Pacific bird sanctuary where the Air Force proposed building a pair of landing pads for cargo delivery tests. However, those plans were suspended in July 2025 amid environmental concerns, and the status of the search for an alternative site is unclear.

item.title: Matrix takes sovereign messaging into the realm of the tech giants
item.description: Decentralized messaging platform Matrix is no longer the upstart it once was. The organization is now a serious challenger to the status quo as concerns about sovereignty and independence reach new heights. At the organization's recent Malmo event, which grew attendance 30 percent year-on-year, the mood shifted from "yes, this is important" to "yes, we're rolling this out." Matrix is an open standard for communication. It's a federated system, so there are no central hubs or overseas control to worry about, and it can be used for anything from messaging to voice over IP. Video is also supported. The system is an alternative to services such as Microsoft Teams. It has become popular in the public sector as governments grow increasingly wary of relying on US tech giants for services that the Trump administration could switch off at will . However, that increased interest and subsequent roll-outs have brought a level of scrutiny Matrix was not fully prepared for. A recent report regarding anonymous reaction to a roll-out of the technology by the European Commission took Element - the company that puts the lion share of the money into Matrix - by surprise. One attendee at the Malmo conference observed, "First they [competitors] ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you." Matrix remains an open standard, however, the open source foundation behind it would certainly welcome more paying members. "It's true that we're definitely getting more attention than we have had before," said Element CEO Matthew Hodgson. "We are seeing Matrix ending up on the critical path of digital sovereignty as almost the poster child of the whole thing. "I'm not sure that we necessarily do want to be the poster child," he added, "We didn't sign up to end up being ambassadors for digital sovereignty, roaming from government to government, but empirically that's where we've ended up, and yeah, that's going to attract attention from people who would rather everyone just kept in their traditional big tech systems." This comes amid worries about the reliability of international partners, from early projects including France's Tchap messenger for the public sector and Germany's BundesMessenger through to more recent users, such as the Swedish public sector. Indeed, in one memorable demonstration during the Matrix event, messages were sent between French, Swedish, and NATO entities. "I cannot overstate the strangeness," Hodgson added, "of having various national militaries phoning up every couple of days, saying, 'Look, we need to get on board Matrix too because we need to talk to this country and they're using Matrix, and we need to talk to that country, and they're using Matrix.'" "It could be for defense, could be national security, could just be healthcare or education, public sector. But that is real. That is why there is a feeding frenzy." item.dc:creator: Richard Speed
item.content:encoded: Decentralized messaging platform Matrix is no longer the upstart it once was. The organization is now a serious challenger to the status quo as concerns about sovereignty and independence reach new heights. At the organization's recent Malmo event, which grew attendance 30 percent year-on-year, the mood shifted from "yes, this is important" to "yes, we're rolling this out." Matrix is an open standard for communication. It's a federated system, so there are no central hubs or overseas control to worry about, and it can be used for anything from messaging to voice over IP. Video is also supported. The system is an alternative to services such as Microsoft Teams. It has become popular in the public sector as governments grow increasingly wary of relying on US tech giants for services that the Trump administration could switch off at will . However, that increased interest and subsequent roll-outs have brought a level of scrutiny Matrix was not fully prepared for. A recent report regarding anonymous reaction to a roll-out of the technology by the European Commission took Element - the company that puts the lion share of the money into Matrix - by surprise. One attendee at the Malmo conference observed, "First they [competitors] ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you." Matrix remains an open standard, however, the open source foundation behind it would certainly welcome more paying members. "It's true that we're definitely getting more attention than we have had before," said Element CEO Matthew Hodgson. "We are seeing Matrix ending up on the critical path of digital sovereignty as almost the poster child of the whole thing. "I'm not sure that we necessarily do want to be the poster child," he added, "We didn't sign up to end up being ambassadors for digital sovereignty, roaming from government to government, but empirically that's where we've ended up, and yeah, that's going to attract attention from people who would rather everyone just kept in their traditional big tech systems." This comes amid worries about the reliability of international partners, from early projects including France's Tchap messenger for the public sector and Germany's BundesMessenger through to more recent users, such as the Swedish public sector. Indeed, in one memorable demonstration during the Matrix event, messages were sent between French, Swedish, and NATO entities. "I cannot overstate the strangeness," Hodgson added, "of having various national militaries phoning up every couple of days, saying, 'Look, we need to get on board Matrix too because we need to talk to this country and they're using Matrix, and we need to talk to that country, and they're using Matrix.'" "It could be for defense, could be national security, could just be healthcare or education, public sector. But that is real. That is why there is a feeding frenzy." Not that Element or Matrix is trying to build a better Teams than Teams. Patrick Alberts, Element's Chief Product Officer, said, "This is a digitally sovereign communication solution that, by and large, works like Teams in many aspects, but it's not set out to be the faster Porsche here..." As for the reported complaints from the European Commission over Element's software implementation, Diana Gheorghe, EC head of sector for Communication and Collaboration Services, addressed them directly and described the anonymous complaints as "the natural friction of [a] high-profile rollout that we have done at scale." Alexandru Vignide, EC service manager for Communication and Collaboration Services, who is very much at the pointy end of making the sovereign communication tools work, noted the speed of the rollout, which began with a proof of concept in Q4 2025, and hit laptops between July and September 2026. The EC chose the Schengen Cloud Alliance (which includes OVHcloud) for hosting and, according to Vignide, "We wanted to provide a familiar experience for users." Not everyone is impressed with what is rolling out , but it's important to remember that change can be alarming, and this is still early days. It is, however, a significant one. Gheorghe said that, as well as increasing resilience and business continuity, "We wanted to have vendor diversity. We also wanted to have data control and ownership of the platform." Microsoft, as an example, would point to the sovereign capabilities of its system. As the Matrix conference kicked off, it announced new capabilities , including additional options for running AI, data services, and confidential workloads on customer-controlled platforms, and highlighted its sovereign partner ecosystem for customers who prefer local expertise. However, Microsoft (and other tech giants) cannot escape concerns about who ultimately controls the data and what administrations might do with it. In 2025, a Microsoft representative memorably confirmed the US giant " cannot guarantee " data sovereignty to customers in France. There is, however, a fly in the Matrix ointment. The platform is open source and, like so many open source projects, requires funding. Right now, Element accounts for much of the Matrix Foundation's funding. Hodgson finds this a little frustrating. "If every government who is operationally dependent on Matrix put the smallest amount of money in the Foundation, the Foundation would have enough money to really start investing in the ecosystem and not be dependent on Element basically picking up the tab." He acknowledged that things had improved in the last year, but said, "It's not good governance for an open standard to have one big player like Element effectively propping things up." This isn't uncommon in the open source world , and it's a little disappointing given the ever-increasing importance placed on sovereignty in communications. Alberts commented: "There is confusion in the market that the thing somehow creates itself. "No, it doesn't. It requires hardworking people. These hardworking people need to be paid, and that payment, in order to support government deployments going forward, ideally also comes from these governments. And some of them do a lot and do it in a great way, and that's amazing. "But some don't." ®

item.title: Google Pay Now Available to Visa Card Holders in Nigeria for Fast, Secure Digital Payments
item.description: Visa , one of the world’s leaders in digital payments, applauds the launch of Google Pay by participating financial institutions in Nigeria, supported through Visa’s partnership with Google . Eligible Visa cardholders of participating financial institutions can now securely add their cards to Google Wallet and make fast, convenient, and secure payments across millions of contactless acceptance points and online merchants. The launch by participating financial institutions marks another significant milestone in Nigeria’s digital payments journey, providing consumers with a simple and secure way to pay using their Android devices. By adding their eligible Visa cards to Google Wallet, users can tap to pay in stores, make purchases online, and enjoy a seamless payment experience across Google’s ecosystem. Google Pay uses tokenization technology to help protect payment information. Instead of storing or sharing a customer’s card number during transactions, a unique digital token is used, providing an additional layer of security while maintaining a fast and convenient checkout experience. As consumer demand for digital-first payment experiences continues to grow, the partnership between Visa and Google, working alongside Nigerian financial institutions, aims to support contactless payment adoption and provide Nigerians with more ways to pay securely wherever Visa contactless payments are accepted. “At Visa, we are committed to advancing the future of payments by delivering innovative, secure, and seamless payment experiences for consumers across Nigeria and beyond . Through our partnership with Google, we are pleased to support our financial institution partners as they bring Google Pay to their cardholders, combining the security of Visa’s global payment network with the convenience consumers increasingly expect in a digital-first world. Helping more people pay with confidence using their mobile devices supports digital commerce, financial inclusion, and the continued growth of Nigeria’s digital economy,” said Andrew Uaboi , Vice President and Cluster Head, Visa West Africa . “We are delighted to bring Google Wallet to Nigeria, a market at the forefront of financial innovation in Africa. Google Wallet makes everyday transactions faster and safer while removing the friction of carrying physical cards. By working alongside Nigeria’s leading financial institutions, we are expanding access to modern digital payment tools for millions of everyday consumers,” said Olumide Balogun , Country Director, Google West Africa About Visa Visa (NYSE: V) is a world leader in digital payments, facilitating transactions between consumers, sellers, financial institutions and government entities across more than 200 countries and territories. Our mission is to connect the world through the most innovative, convenient, reliable, and secure payments network, enabling individuals, businesses, and economies to thrive. item.title: Admin dropped the F-bomb in a password to show hackers who was really 1337
item.description: Welcome back to PWNED, in which The Reg offers cautionary tales from folks who’ve left their doors wide open to attackers and lived to tell the tale. This week’s misadventure involves unpatched older machines and a password that was supposed to send a message to crims. Our story comes courtesy once again of leading red teamer and pen tester Dahvid Schloss of Suzu Labs . A client asked Schloss to visit a factory and check the servers there for security holes. The company had been hacked six months prior, made some adjustments, and wanted to make sure that they were bulletproof now. Schloss' mission, which he chose to accept, was to get domain admin rights. Schloss drove over to the factory where he noticed a number of Windows 7 servers were connected to the CNC milling machines, even though Windows 10 was by then Microsoft's supported desktop OS. This was to be expected, as companies with proprietary software often use legacy OSes for fear of breaking apps. At first, Schloss had a hard time breaking in because most of the servers were not connected to the domain. So there was no point in his running the EternalBlue zero-day that would have let him in. “So I've been looking through these and most of them had been disconnected from the domain, so it's the right move,” he said. “Like, yeah, you could run EternalBlue on the network, but you really weren't going to be able to get anywhere with it, cuz you get on the device and what you find: you dump LSASS [the Windows Local Security Authority Subsystem Service], you’re like ‘All right, there’s local admin creds, but the local admin creds on those devices were different from the local admin creds on the majority of workstations.” Finally, Schloss went onto one of the servers that was connected to milling machines and found that it was connected to the network and on the domain. It was vulnerable to EternalBlue and he went and dumped LSASS and found a pair of creds from WDigest, one of which looked like an admin account. But Schloss thought that it must not be a legitimate admin account when he read the password : “heyhackergof***yourself,” but written in leet speak [ l337 5p34k ]. The resulting string was a strong password, but Schloss assumed that the admins were playing a game with him and left this credential there for him to find. item.dc:creator: Avram Piltch
item.content:encoded: Welcome back to PWNED, in which The Reg offers cautionary tales from folks who’ve left their doors wide open to attackers and lived to tell the tale. This week’s misadventure involves unpatched older machines and a password that was supposed to send a message to crims. Our story comes courtesy once again of leading red teamer and pen tester Dahvid Schloss of Suzu Labs . A client asked Schloss to visit a factory and check the servers there for security holes. The company had been hacked six months prior, made some adjustments, and wanted to make sure that they were bulletproof now. Schloss' mission, which he chose to accept, was to get domain admin rights. Schloss drove over to the factory where he noticed a number of Windows 7 servers were connected to the CNC milling machines, even though Windows 10 was by then Microsoft's supported desktop OS. This was to be expected, as companies with proprietary software often use legacy OSes for fear of breaking apps. At first, Schloss had a hard time breaking in because most of the servers were not connected to the domain. So there was no point in his running the EternalBlue zero-day that would have let him in. “So I've been looking through these and most of them had been disconnected from the domain, so it's the right move,” he said. “Like, yeah, you could run EternalBlue on the network, but you really weren't going to be able to get anywhere with it, cuz you get on the device and what you find: you dump LSASS [the Windows Local Security Authority Subsystem Service], you’re like ‘All right, there’s local admin creds, but the local admin creds on those devices were different from the local admin creds on the majority of workstations.” Finally, Schloss went onto one of the servers that was connected to milling machines and found that it was connected to the network and on the domain. It was vulnerable to EternalBlue and he went and dumped LSASS and found a pair of creds from WDigest, one of which looked like an admin account. But Schloss thought that it must not be a legitimate admin account when he read the password : “heyhackergof***yourself,” but written in leet speak [ l337 5p34k ]. The resulting string was a strong password, but Schloss assumed that the admins were playing a game with him and left this credential there for him to find. Schloss assumed it wouldn't work and sat on it for a week. During a briefing he had with the IT crew, he presented his findings and then asked who set up the admin account with this funny password. “You could see everyone kind of looking at the senior manager of IT like ‘that was you, wasn’t it,’” Schloss explained. “He’s kind of got this face. I’m like ‘oh shit, like what?’ Turns out that ‘heyhackergof***yourself’ was the actual password for his admin account." On Monday, Schloss tried the username and password combo and, lo and behold, it gave him complete control of the entire network. He was then able to get access to other passwords and many of them were also insults directed at potential hackers. Schloss understood that the team was still angry about a breach they had suffered six months prior and, should they be breached again, wanted to give the finger to the hacker who did it. Unfortunately, their system was still vulnerable because of the outdated machine that was hooked up to the domain and he was able to gain control. The lesson here is really to patch your systems and avoid using insecure legacy OSes whenever possible, because it was an old machine that let Schloss in, not a weak password. Indeed, “hackergof***yourself” in leet speak isn’t a terrible password, just an embarrassing one if it's exposed. ®

item.title: HPE puts storage to work on AI’s expensive memory problem
item.description: HPE is giving its Alletra Storage MP X10000 another job: holding inference state that would otherwise be evicted from expensive GPU memory and recalculated later. In testing validated by Kamiwaza using NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the Kamiwaza AI platform, and HPE Alletra MP X10000, the solution achieved up to 20× faster time to first token and 17× higher effective inference throughput versus running without KV cache offload. The GPUs did not become cleverer. They had less repeat work to do. The results move a storage decision directly into the discussion about AI economics. Model pricing gets plenty of attention. Paying expensive accelerators to process the same context repeatedly deserves some too. Especially as enterprises move from chatbots answering individual questions to agents that can turn one request into a small committee’s worth of activity. Your agents have a repetition problem Agentic workflows repeatedly process documents, system instructions and conversation histories. One agent retrieves information, another evaluates it, a third checks the result, and subsequent steps revisit material the system has already processed. Some repetition is necessary. Recalculating everything is not. KV cache retains intermediate attention state, allowing compatible requests to reuse earlier computation. Keeping that cache available can reduce the work required before a model starts producing its next answer. GPU memory, unfortunately, is neither infinite nor priced as though it were. Long contexts and concurrent sessions compete for that memory. When reusable cache is evicted and later needed, the inference engine may have to rebuild it. More GPU work, more waiting, and no additional insight to show for either. HPE Alletra MP X10000 provides a shared tier for offloaded cache, while RDMA for S3 accelerates the storage data path. The proposition: retrieve reusable context rather than make the GPU calculate it again. Compute once. Reuse often. An unremarkable principle, until the alternative appears on the infrastructure bill. Twenty times faster, with the denominator attached The Kamiwaza-validated testing used NVIDIA Nemotron 70B and more than 30 concurrent agents under large-context, multi-agent inference. That matters because this is precisely the sort of real-world workload where repeated context and memory pressure can make cache reuse valuable. Several agents consulting overlapping material create a different opportunity from unrelated, short prompts with little context in common. Those headline gains are workload-specific. Context length, concurrency, cache hit rates and transfer overhead determine the return. Twenty times faster is a test result, not a universal entitlement. Buyers should examine the comparison as carefully as the multiplier: the same workload, with and without KV cache offload, and enough concurrency to represent production conditions. The useful question is how much repeated computation their applications can avoid, and whether retrie
item.dc:creator: Colin Gallagher
item.content:encoded: HPE is giving its Alletra Storage MP X10000 another job: holding inference state that would otherwise be evicted from expensive GPU memory and recalculated later. In testing validated by Kamiwaza using NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the Kamiwaza AI platform, and HPE Alletra MP X10000, the solution achieved up to 20× faster time to first token and 17× higher effective inference throughput versus running without KV cache offload. The GPUs did not become cleverer. They had less repeat work to do. The results move a storage decision directly into the discussion about AI economics. Model pricing gets plenty of attention. Paying expensive accelerators to process the same context repeatedly deserves some too. Especially as enterprises move from chatbots answering individual questions to agents that can turn one request into a small committee’s worth of activity. Your agents have a repetition problem Agentic workflows repeatedly process documents, system instructions and conversation histories. One agent retrieves information, another evaluates it, a third checks the result, and subsequent steps revisit material the system has already processed. Some repetition is necessary. Recalculating everything is not. KV cache retains intermediate attention state, allowing compatible requests to reuse earlier computation. Keeping that cache available can reduce the work required before a model starts producing its next answer. GPU memory, unfortunately, is neither infinite nor priced as though it were. Long contexts and concurrent sessions compete for that memory. When reusable cache is evicted and later needed, the inference engine may have to rebuild it. More GPU work, more waiting, and no additional insight to show for either. HPE Alletra MP X10000 provides a shared tier for offloaded cache, while RDMA for S3 accelerates the storage data path. The proposition: retrieve reusable context rather than make the GPU calculate it again. Compute once. Reuse often. An unremarkable principle, until the alternative appears on the infrastructure bill. Twenty times faster, with the denominator attached The Kamiwaza-validated testing used NVIDIA Nemotron 70B and more than 30 concurrent agents under large-context, multi-agent inference. That matters because this is precisely the sort of real-world workload where repeated context and memory pressure can make cache reuse valuable. Several agents consulting overlapping material create a different opportunity from unrelated, short prompts with little context in common. Those headline gains are workload-specific. Context length, concurrency, cache hit rates and transfer overhead determine the return. Twenty times faster is a test result, not a universal entitlement. Buyers should examine the comparison as carefully as the multiplier: the same workload, with and without KV cache offload, and enough concurrency to represent production conditions. The useful question is how much repeated computation their applications can avoid, and whether retrieving cached context is faster than rebuilding it. A large performance number without its test conditions is mostly a typography decision. Garbage in still costs money Cache reuse addresses repeated computation. It cannot rescue a retrieval system that feeds the model half the company’s document archive to answer one question. HPE’s broader pitch pairs the X10000 with Data Fabric for governed access to distributed data. The X10000’s data intelligence node generates metadata, classification and embeddings at ingest to help applications retrieve relevant context. That moves preparation closer to where data lands, rather than leaving every application team to assemble another downstream preparation pipeline. The economic logic is straightforward. More precise retrieval can mean less irrelevant material in prompts and fewer attempts to obtain a useful answer. Enterprise archives are rarely short of documents. Distinguishing the current policy from six superseded versions and a presentation called “FINAL_final_v7” is the more interesting problem. Governance also matters when agents retrieve information and act on it. Relevant context still needs to be authorized context. Faster access to something an agent should never have seen is an awkward definition of progress. That gives HPE two economic levers: improve what enters inference, then reuse computation where possible. The distinction matters. Better retrieval can reduce prompt size and retries. KV cache reuse reduces processing work; it does not magically shrink generated answers or oblige an API supplier to lower its bill. Beyond the cache checkbox Cache offload is becoming a crowded market. HPE’s strength rests on combining it with data preparation and governance, rather than winning another feature tick. The practical test for organizations looking to get more value from their AI is how smoothly data preparation, governance and cache reuse operate as a single system. Can applications find relevant, permitted information without unnecessary copying and preparation? Can the inference engine retain and retrieve reusable context efficiently? Does the combination sustain useful throughput as context windows and agent counts grow? Those questions connect the architecture to observable outcomes. Buyers should ask for cache hit rates, time to first token and sustained throughput on their workloads. They should also examine retrieval quality and whether the system completes the intended task. A faster wrong answer remains a wrong answer, however attractive the benchmark chart. Cost per terabyte remains relevant. So does the cost of making a GPU read the same briefing for the seventh time. For more information, visit the HPE Alletra Storage MP X10000 web page . Contributed by HPE
