item.title: Our verdict on Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel: Not her best book
item.description: The New Scientist Book Club read Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel in October Author image: Laura Barisonzi After a deep dive into particle physics in September with cosmologist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein’s non-fiction title The Edge of Space-Time , in October the New Scientist Book Club stuck with physics but made it fictional, with Emily St. John Mandel’s new speculative fiction novel Exit Party . Set in the near future, this is a tale involving quantum entanglement and parallel worlds, but Mandel being Mandel, it’s much more a tale of the people who live in those worlds than the physics that makes them possible. Our sci-fi columnist Emily H. Wilson gave it a glowing review , saying Exit Party was “as elegant and brilliantly executed as [Mandel’s] fans will have grown to expect”. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter The book starts in Los Angeles in 2031 in the aftermath of civil war, as the curfew lifts and our protagonist Ari, recently released after years in prison, sets out for a party. She and her friends see some mysterious doppelgangers at the party, but the mystery isn’t really resolved until the second half of the book. By then, we’ve followed Ari through the anarchy and chaos of this lawless version of the US, and we discover that another version of the future is also unspooling. Advertisement I asked Emily (Mandel, that is) what it was like to write about her imagined near-future US when we chatted. “By the time I finished the book, I felt like I was struggling to stay ahead of the American news cycle,” she told me. “In 2022 [when she started writing], the notion of masked police seizing people off the streets or shooting civilians in broad daylight would have seemed quite fantastical, but those were literally the ICE raids in Minneapolis.” I adored the novel Mandel is most famous for, Station Eleven , another imagined near-future but this time set in the aftermath of a flu pandemic. I agree with Emily (Wilson, that is) that this latest is just as beautifully and brilliantly written, but I wasn’t quite as compelled by it, at least for the first half of the novel. By the time we got to the second half, the drama and the science fictional elements ramped up and I ended up really enjoying it, but it’s never that great to press a book on a friend with the words “just give it 100 pages…”. Book club members, chatting on Discord as they read, were equally conflicted. “Just finished Exit Party . Not, IMO, Mandel’s best book,” wrote Tethysnz. “When I finished Sea of Tranquility , I went back and reread it right away to understand all the connections and undercurrents I’d missed. But with Exit Party connections are pretty clear and not all that interesting.” Alan_P felt similarly to me about the first half – it’s “almost without incident except for the actual odd appearances and disappearances”, he wrote. “The pace does pick up a little in the final quarter of the book, but most of it is a beautifully described descriptio
item.dc:creator: Alison Flood
item.content:encoded: The New Scientist Book Club read Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel in October Author image: Laura Barisonzi After a deep dive into particle physics in September with cosmologist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein’s non-fiction title The Edge of Space-Time , in October the New Scientist Book Club stuck with physics but made it fictional, with Emily St. John Mandel’s new speculative fiction novel Exit Party . Set in the near future, this is a tale involving quantum entanglement and parallel worlds, but Mandel being Mandel, it’s much more a tale of the people who live in those worlds than the physics that makes them possible. Our sci-fi columnist Emily H. Wilson gave it a glowing review , saying Exit Party was “as elegant and brilliantly executed as [Mandel’s] fans will have grown to expect”. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter The book starts in Los Angeles in 2031 in the aftermath of civil war, as the curfew lifts and our protagonist Ari, recently released after years in prison, sets out for a party. She and her friends see some mysterious doppelgangers at the party, but the mystery isn’t really resolved until the second half of the book. By then, we’ve followed Ari through the anarchy and chaos of this lawless version of the US, and we discover that another version of the future is also unspooling. Advertisement I asked Emily (Mandel, that is) what it was like to write about her imagined near-future US when we chatted. “By the time I finished the book, I felt like I was struggling to stay ahead of the American news cycle,” she told me. “In 2022 [when she started writing], the notion of masked police seizing people off the streets or shooting civilians in broad daylight would have seemed quite fantastical, but those were literally the ICE raids in Minneapolis.” I adored the novel Mandel is most famous for, Station Eleven , another imagined near-future but this time set in the aftermath of a flu pandemic. I agree with Emily (Wilson, that is) that this latest is just as beautifully and brilliantly written, but I wasn’t quite as compelled by it, at least for the first half of the novel. By the time we got to the second half, the drama and the science fictional elements ramped up and I ended up really enjoying it, but it’s never that great to press a book on a friend with the words “just give it 100 pages…”. Book club members, chatting on Discord as they read, were equally conflicted. “Just finished Exit Party . Not, IMO, Mandel’s best book,” wrote Tethysnz. “When I finished Sea of Tranquility , I went back and reread it right away to understand all the connections and undercurrents I’d missed. But with Exit Party connections are pretty clear and not all that interesting.” Alan_P felt similarly to me about the first half – it’s “almost without incident except for the actual odd appearances and disappearances”, he wrote. “The pace does pick up a little in the final quarter of the book, but most of it is a beautifully described description of two very different societies,” he added. “It’s a good book – I don’t think it’s a great book but it is technically very good, and has an interesting ending. But it makes you work to get there and I don’t think that improves it.” Matthew found Mandel’s writing style “overly careful, which gets in the way. Which isn’t to say she isn’t a very good writer, perhaps she just needs to let her hair down a bit”, while PiriShepherd, conversely, really enjoyed the novel’s opening. “I love the idea that a party is the place where the unintended bridge between universes opens up. A party is disorientating – somewhere you might be a bit drunk – where unexpected or inexplicable things happen – where people show up that you didn’t expect to see,” they wrote. “Where there might be consequences or disastrous events that extend beyond the next morning.” “There’s such an intriguing start but then the mystery is largely left aside for a long time – possibly too long for the reader’s satisfaction?” said Dee55. “I found the book’s B part much more gripping – and disturbingly close to things that are already happening in some countries.” Katita2026 found Mandel’s future visions very frightening. “She doesn’t give us a ‘bad world’ and a ‘good world.’ She gives us the two greatest political nightmares of the 21st century,” Katita wrote, pondering if “the genius (and the terror) of this book lies precisely in this political pessimism”. “By offering a world torn between absolute chaos and absolute tyranny, isn’t the author diagnosing that modern society has already lost the ability to imagine a future where democracy survives?” Katita asked. As you can see, book club members really put this thoughtful, thought-provoking novel through the wringer!

item.title: The King’s Observatory could be yours for the low, low price of £18 million
item.description: Josie Ford Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more Observe this listing Feedback has, belatedly in life, stumbled upon a new life interest: wildly aspirational property choices. We previously highlighted the Farnborough Centrifuge, a piece of aviation and space-flight history now up for sale as a home for someone with £750,000 to burn. The Centrifuge was still available the last time we checked. Now, chief subeditor Kelsey Hayes has identified an even more expensive domicile up for sale, which has been highlighted by the news site London Centric . Compared with this, she notes, the Farnborough Centrifuge “now seems like a bargain”. When Feedback opened the tab for the listing , it announced at the top: “Four bedroom detached house for sale”. While this is technically true, it does not quite capture the scale of the property in question. Advertisement What is up for sale is the King’s Observatory in Old Deer Park, London. It is a former astronomical observatory, since converted into a private home. It was built on the orders of King George III (as in The Madness of ) in the 1760s, so that he and his wife Queen Charlotte (as in Bridgerton ) could observe the 1769 transit of Venus. At the time, this was a major scientific endeavour, because it offered a way to determine the distance from Earth to the sun. Evidently the royals wanted to share the excitement. Careful examination of the listing reveals that the observatory is still operational: one of the photos shows an antique wood and brass telescope housed inside a cupola. Kelsey notes with bemusement that the estate agents do not seem to regard this as a major selling point: “it’s the last photo in the slideshow”. In the decades after the transit, the observatory was used for an array of scientific tasks , including measuring atmospheric electricity and verifying the accuracy of instruments such as clocks. In the 1980s, it became offices, and in the 21st century, a private home. The listing describes it as having not a garden, but “grounds”, and a drive that can accommodate the adjective “sweeping”. Grecian carp are mentioned. At this point, Feedback had heard enough. We were poised to book a viewing when we noticed the asking price: £18 million. We find ourselves a tad short. We could try for a mortgage, but we fear that by definition it would be sub-prime. London Centric did highlight one potential disadvantage of purchasing the King’s Observatory: “You do, however, have to live in the middle of a golf course.” Readers and their spouses will have their own views as to whether this is a plus or a minus. Dust to dust We continue our efforts to compile the most niche science-themed tourist attractions from around the world. In this we have been aided by Brian Reffin Smith, who alerts us to “an exceptional wonder”: the Museum of Dust. The museum is the creation of artist and author Sally Kindberg . It’s a little cabinet , blue

item.content:encoded: Josie Ford Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more Observe this listing Feedback has, belatedly in life, stumbled upon a new life interest: wildly aspirational property choices. We previously highlighted the Farnborough Centrifuge, a piece of aviation and space-flight history now up for sale as a home for someone with £750,000 to burn. The Centrifuge was still available the last time we checked. Now, chief subeditor Kelsey Hayes has identified an even more expensive domicile up for sale, which has been highlighted by the news site London Centric . Compared with this, she notes, the Farnborough Centrifuge “now seems like a bargain”. When Feedback opened the tab for the listing , it announced at the top: “Four bedroom detached house for sale”. While this is technically true, it does not quite capture the scale of the property in question. Advertisement What is up for sale is the King’s Observatory in Old Deer Park, London. It is a former astronomical observatory, since converted into a private home. It was built on the orders of King George III (as in The Madness of ) in the 1760s, so that he and his wife Queen Charlotte (as in Bridgerton ) could observe the 1769 transit of Venus. At the time, this was a major scientific endeavour, because it offered a way to determine the distance from Earth to the sun. Evidently the royals wanted to share the excitement. Careful examination of the listing reveals that the observatory is still operational: one of the photos shows an antique wood and brass telescope housed inside a cupola. Kelsey notes with bemusement that the estate agents do not seem to regard this as a major selling point: “it’s the last photo in the slideshow”. In the decades after the transit, the observatory was used for an array of scientific tasks , including measuring atmospheric electricity and verifying the accuracy of instruments such as clocks. In the 1980s, it became offices, and in the 21st century, a private home. The listing describes it as having not a garden, but “grounds”, and a drive that can accommodate the adjective “sweeping”. Grecian carp are mentioned. At this point, Feedback had heard enough. We were poised to book a viewing when we noticed the asking price: £18 million. We find ourselves a tad short. We could try for a mortgage, but we fear that by definition it would be sub-prime. London Centric did highlight one potential disadvantage of purchasing the King’s Observatory: “You do, however, have to live in the middle of a golf course.” Readers and their spouses will have their own views as to whether this is a plus or a minus. Dust to dust We continue our efforts to compile the most niche science-themed tourist attractions from around the world. In this we have been aided by Brian Reffin Smith, who alerts us to “an exceptional wonder”: the Museum of Dust. The museum is the creation of artist and author Sally Kindberg . It’s a little cabinet , blue on the outside and red inside. It’s divided into eight compartments: two across, four down. Each houses an array of little bottles of dust. But not just any dust. Sally has gathered samples from around the world. There is dust from the Great Wall of China and from the wrapping of an ancient Egyptian mummy. Another sample comes from yet another museum, the self-explanatory House of Automata. Do not look at photos of the items on display at the House of Automata unless you want to be inspired to write a M3GAN -style horror movie. Sometimes people send Sally dust, which must surely cause a brief frisson of alarm when she opens the envelope. She has dust from the TARDIS from Doctor Who , sent to her in 2013 by a friend who worked on the show. She also has a sample of dust from the 2007 Celebrity Big Brother house, but has not yet revealed how she obtained it. Readers eager to see the Museum of Dust need to know it has no permanent home: instead you have to attend one of Sally’s workshops or talks . Just try not to sneeze. Not in a name Occasionally Feedback likes to throw a spanner in the works. In that spirit, we will highlight some examples of what we might call anti-nominative determinism: that is, people whose names are the opposite of what we might expect given their jobs. In Queropalca, a remote district of Peru, a recent mayoral election was won by a candidate named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores. That name contains two waving red flags, but, in fact, Hitler Mussolini is a member of the Ahora NaciÓn party, which is on the centre-left. This sort of thing seems to happen quite a lot in South America. For instance, between 2017 and 2021, the president of Ecuador was one Lenín Moreno . Elected as a social democrat, he pivoted to right-wing economic policies – none of which, one feels, the original Lenin would have approved of. Likewise, reader Hillary Shaw wrote in to highlight another example of inappropriate naming: the 19th-century poet William Jeffrey Prowse. This one took Feedback a moment to understand because we associate the surname Prowse with the actor who embodied Darth Vader, whereas Hillary simply wanted us to read it without the “w”. Meanwhile, in Australia, Bonita Ely was alarmed to discover that her next cancer check-up was with a “Dr Kilian”. Got a story for Feedback? You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist.com . Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website .

item.title: Cadillac Escalade IQ review: Huge battery, huge range, huge SUV
item.description: “Please have at least 125 miles of range left when we pick it up.” That request from the people who look after the Cadillac press cars wasn’t going to be hard to honor. The electric Escalade IQ arrived with an indicated range of 440 miles (708 km), and with a full week of work to squeeze in, getting anywhere close to needing to recharge it seemed unlikely. With more than 200 kWh of lithium-ion battery between its axles, range is one thing the big electric Caddy needn’t worry about. Designed and debuted during a time of greater EV optimism, the Escalade is Cadillac’s statement that swapping out a V8 for a pair of powerful electric motors is no compromise to its ambitions, even if the brand’s future will now include a mix of electric and combustion cars beyond 2030 . It shares a battery pack and much else with other full-size GM EVs we’ve tested: the Chevrolet Silverado EV , the GMC Sierra EV , and of course the divisive Hummer EVs . And like those trucks and SUVs, the Escalade is large and heavy—just small enough to fit into a standard parking space, with a curb weight sufficient to push it into the Class 3 truck category. So, the side mirrors are flat, and there’s no formal EPA range—Cadillac says it achieves 460 miles (740 km) on the EPA test cycle—but there are plenty of airbags, even though the 9,046 lb (4,103 kg) curb weight does not require them. Yes, you did read that right, it does weigh 4 tons. And yes, the electric Escalade does weigh a third more than the last gas-powered one we tested . Read full article Comments

item.title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
item.description: If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden's win that November. If you ask Google's AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources. When I put the direct question of "Who won the 2020 presidential election?" to Google's AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media ), I got the following surprisingly indirect response: "To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC)." My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google's AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project's 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000. Read full article Comments

item.title: Florida county won’t investigate sketchy Flock cameras removed by mystery owners
item.description: A Florida county that discovered a clump of mysterious unpermitted Flock cameras during a countywide takedown effort won’t investigate who owned the sketchy cameras, which have since disappeared. On Wednesday, The Washington Post reported that St. Lucie County residents "remain upset,” not knowing who installed the cameras or how they were using the data collected. Hannah Galindo, a 31-year-old resident who petitioned to get Flock cameras removed, told the Post that she was worried “that data could be anywhere.” Of the 12 cameras found, five were eventually claimed by city law enforcement, the Post reported. Apparently, a police department mistakenly issued guidance claiming that officers could post multiple cameras under one permit, a Flock spokesperson told the Post, even though the county required individual permits. However, neither Flock nor the city police departments in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce that claimed the sketchy cameras will confirm who gave the guidance. Read full article Comments

item.title: Amazon tells tokenmaxxing devs to slow their AI roll
item.description: Maximize value, not token usage, Amazon has told its engineers, citing concerns about rising AI costs and complexity. Amazon made the strategy shift public on Tuesday in a note to engineering teams outlining the changing role of its software development engineers in the age of AI. “Our most prolific engineers have demonstrated that neither the developer role nor their output is defined by the use of AI,” Amazon VP and distinguished engineer Terk Terkowitz wrote in the note. “We're now in the era of the Renaissance Developer, blending AI tools with human judgment and domain expertise to build entirely new things.” In other words, Amazon wants its developers using AI, but burning through tokens isn't the same thing as getting useful work done. Rather than define the developer role by how AI is used, the memo focuses on what isn't changing so fast: the need to deliver useful software and results for customers and the business. “It is difficult to define, in a way that will stand the test of time, what good AI powered engineering practices look like,” the memo continues. “We have decided to focus on what is not changing as we evolved the SDE roles … the outcomes that matter aren’t changing, even if the inputs, tools, and techniques are changing faster than ever.” What that means for software developers in the present moment is that AI input metrics, even if Amazon has seen some correlation with increased productivity and delivery on tokenmaxxing teams, aren’t what Amazon sees as a measurement of good use of developer time and resources. “We are all aware of how deeply flawed these metrics are, primarily because they are disconnected from what matters,” the memo argues. “[U]sing these metrics could, if used as a target instead of a measure, drive negative outcomes, increasing costs, and increasing complexity,” the memo continues, referring to tokenmaxxing costs and overly complex code that’s at odds with Amazon’s mission to “invent and simplify.” An Amazon spokesperson confirmed that the memo’s intent was to discourage tokenmaxxing, pointing us to comments from AWS CEO Matt Garman from June in which he encouraged developers to measure outcomes, not token consumption, in making proper use of AI tools for software development. Amazon also wants its developers thinking more about how AI can help “improve delivery for customers” and business units, not just trying to find a place to stick it to prove it's working for them. The memo calls out some engineering teams who’ve “become less connected to their customers and business,” and says teams that are more engaged with their products and business roles “are able to take the most advantage of AI and agentic software development,” in essence calling for more teams to take a similar approach. “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the memo said. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking fo
item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: Maximize value, not token usage, Amazon has told its engineers, citing concerns about rising AI costs and complexity. Amazon made the strategy shift public on Tuesday in a note to engineering teams outlining the changing role of its software development engineers in the age of AI. “Our most prolific engineers have demonstrated that neither the developer role nor their output is defined by the use of AI,” Amazon VP and distinguished engineer Terk Terkowitz wrote in the note. “We're now in the era of the Renaissance Developer, blending AI tools with human judgment and domain expertise to build entirely new things.” In other words, Amazon wants its developers using AI, but burning through tokens isn't the same thing as getting useful work done. Rather than define the developer role by how AI is used, the memo focuses on what isn't changing so fast: the need to deliver useful software and results for customers and the business. “It is difficult to define, in a way that will stand the test of time, what good AI powered engineering practices look like,” the memo continues. “We have decided to focus on what is not changing as we evolved the SDE roles … the outcomes that matter aren’t changing, even if the inputs, tools, and techniques are changing faster than ever.” What that means for software developers in the present moment is that AI input metrics, even if Amazon has seen some correlation with increased productivity and delivery on tokenmaxxing teams, aren’t what Amazon sees as a measurement of good use of developer time and resources. “We are all aware of how deeply flawed these metrics are, primarily because they are disconnected from what matters,” the memo argues. “[U]sing these metrics could, if used as a target instead of a measure, drive negative outcomes, increasing costs, and increasing complexity,” the memo continues, referring to tokenmaxxing costs and overly complex code that’s at odds with Amazon’s mission to “invent and simplify.” An Amazon spokesperson confirmed that the memo’s intent was to discourage tokenmaxxing, pointing us to comments from AWS CEO Matt Garman from June in which he encouraged developers to measure outcomes, not token consumption, in making proper use of AI tools for software development. Amazon also wants its developers thinking more about how AI can help “improve delivery for customers” and business units, not just trying to find a place to stick it to prove it's working for them. The memo calls out some engineering teams who’ve “become less connected to their customers and business,” and says teams that are more engaged with their products and business roles “are able to take the most advantage of AI and agentic software development,” in essence calling for more teams to take a similar approach. “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the memo said. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.” Amazon's take in the memo is starkly similar to what Microsoft told its own internal development teams in August, right down to stressing a focus on returns for customers and business instead of maximizing input. "Tokenmaxxing is not what we are optimizing for," Microsoft EVP Jay Parikh told developers. "I want all of us focused on maximizing outcomes that move the needle for our customers and our business." With that, the writing seems to be on the wall for the throw-AI-at-everything-and-see-where-it-sticks approach to integrating the tech. When two companies that large start to question whether AI token consumption is a useful measure of productivity for their thousands of software engineers, it's possible the rest of the world will soon start sipping those tokens instead of chugging them. That, or we'll soon see even more enterprises begin to embrace the philosophy of relying on "good enough" open-weight models that can handle many tasks at a fraction of the cost of more expensive alternatives – Garman made a similar case for choosing cost-effective models based on the task back in June. If you're a bubble, that approach looks an awful lot like a pin. ®

item.title: GitHub powering up four million extra cores to stop its service going down
item.description: GitHub's Universe conference kicked off in San Francisco on Wednesday with news that its infrastructural universe is expanding to address staggering demand from AI agents. GitHub recorded 7.4 billion code commits in September 2026, five times more than hit its servers a year earlier. This surge in traffic over the past year, the result of developers running AI agents and generating increased amounts of programming code, caught the company unprepared and led to a series of outages and service availability woes. AI-driven code commits started becoming a problem last December, and led to problems in February , April , August , not to mention the months in between. On May 7, the site's 90-day availability hit a low of about 84 percent , according to reconstructed data from GitHub's status page. GitHub execs apologized and promised to do better. Those commitments have put four million CPU cores and 160 petabytes of high-speed storage on its infrastructure roadmap, alongside extra compute capacity for GitHub Actions, the company's beleaguered continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) platform. The Microsoft-owned code hosting biz also says it is redesigning its technical architecture (an effort discussed previously ) to separate compute and storage, with the expectation that will enable 35x more throughput. "We’re also migrating to a multi-region deployment in Azure , while continuing to serve incredible levels of traffic from developers around the world," said Jay Parikh, EVP of CoreAI, Microsoft, in a blog post provided to The Register . "We expect to complete the migration early next year. Those investments give us more room to grow. The next step is building the systems that handle the work." Also at the its Universe event , GitHub announced general availability of Copilot Fusion, the company's model routing service that was previewed under the name HydraFusion . The idea is that allowing GitHub to route requests to different models can improve task-completion rates while reducing token consumption costs. "Different tasks need different models," said Parikh. "Developers shouldn’t have to manage every model choice to get the right result at the right price. Copilot Fusion evaluates what a task needs across reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use, then chooses how to execute across one or more models. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40% less time per task." GitHub is making more bells and whistles available through its Copilot app, including Copilot Projects, for coordinating parallel work; Copilot Connectors, for simplifying how Copilot connects to MCP servers; and Copilot Automations, which are reusable agent tasks. And in what appears to be an effort to boost Copilot usage in the workplace, GitHub is extending Copilot access to all GitHub Enterprise users without requiring any additional per-seat purchases. Customer still get billed for

Customer still get billed for the tokens they use. Another new offering is a package firewall that checks enterprise policy settings before fetching npm packages. ®

item.title: Football Daily | Fleetwood go their own way to down Arsenal and live Carabao Cup dream
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Having made a passing reference to Mick Fleetwood in Tuesday’s thrilling edition of your favourite email, Football Daily genuinely wasn’t expecting to be repeatedly typing that particular F-word in our lead story in today’s edition. While we were aware Arsenal were in the coastal town of Fleetwood for a Fizzy Cup tie that could scarcely have been less glamorous than the previous evening’s Ballon d’Or ceremony at the Palladium, the needle on our patented Potential Shock-o-Meter had barely moved before a match pitting the Premier League champions against a side struggling in League Two. Even with the residual winds from Storm Boelo still buffeting the ground, we presumed Arsenal’s second string would have enough about them to record a comfortable win at Highbury, over 20 years after they left a London stadium of the same name to begin their residency at the Emirates. It was not to be and almost five months to the day since exiting a cup competition on penalties following a curiously flat and uninspired display, Mikel Arteta’s side exited a cup competition on penalties following etc, and so on. Continue reading...

item.title: How Spiders Spin ‘Silk Dope’ Into Nature’s Toughest Material
item.description: A spider, when knocked off a wall, doesn’t fall for long. Within milliseconds, it spins a soup of proteins into sturdy climbing gear. Using a thin, shimmering strand of silk, the spider hauls itself back up. The strand is tougher than Kevlar, the synthetic fiber in bike tires and bulletproof vests, and stronger than steel. It’s flexible and biocompatible with human bodies. Source

item.title: Serial ransomware crook gets 70 months behind bars for Nefilim, Hive roles
item.description: Ukrainian ransomware crook Artem Stryzhak has been sentenced to 70 months in the slammer by a New York federal court for his role as an affiliate of the Nefilim and Hive ransomware gangs. Prosecutors believe the cybercriminal began working with Nefilim in or around June 2021, while living in Barcelona, Spain. The Nefilim ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was known for targeting wealthy companies, with its operators encouraging affiliates to pursue businesses capable of paying substantial ransom demands. One of Nefilim's most high-profile attacks was on Australian logistics giant Toll Group in 2020, encrypting its files roughly three months after it suffered a separate Mailto ransomware attack. Court documents [PDF] state that Stryzhak agreed with alleged Nefilim boss Volodymyr Tymoshchuk , who remains at large, to pay the ransomware crew a 20 percent cut of the ransom proceeds he collected. Tymoshchuk told Stryzhak that his preference was for attacks to target companies based in the US, Canada, and Australia that turn over more than $100 million annually. This guidance was soon tweaked to encourage targeting companies in the same regions with more than $200 million in annual revenue. Prosecutors claim that around the time Stryzhak joined forces with Nefilim, he also signed up to the Hive ransomware operation as "one of its earliest affiliates," and used its platform to attack approximately seven victims. Hive's operators claimed they targeted circa 1,500 victims worldwide between June 2021 and January 2023. According to separate court documents [PDF], Hive's victims included a law firm and an Ohio hospital, which paid approximately $1.7 million in Bitcoin after the gang initially demanded $2 million during the COVID-19 pandemic. Before its infrastructure was seized in an international law enforcement operation in January 2023, Hive was known for attacking healthcare facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as being one of the ransomware groups that battered Costa Rica in 2022 . Brett Leatherman, assistant director at the FBI’s cyber branch, described Stryzhak as a “prolific cybercriminal” who played a role in groups that were responsible for more than $100 million in victim damages. “Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners,” he said. “Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.” Stryzhak was arrested by Spanish police in June 2024 before being extradited to the US in April 2025. item.title: China's secretive space plane caught on camera in incredible new photo released by US military
item.description: null A photograph of China's reusable Shenlong space plane docked to another spacecraft, taken by Vantor's WorldView 3 satellite from a distance of 56 miles (90 kilometers). (Image credit: Satellite image ©2026 Vantor) A U.S. military intelligence agency has released an incredible new photograph of China's secretive space plane, showing it docked to another spacecraft in orbit. The photograph was taken in 2024 by Vantor's WorldView 3 satellite, from a distance of 56 miles (90 kilometers). Ground-based observers have previously photographed Shenlong in orbit , but this new photo from Vantor, taken from space, reveals new details about the mysterious spacecraft in stunning clarity, with a resolution of 4.5 centimeters (1.8 inches) per pixel. The image was included in a new report released by the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) assessing the scope and breadth of adversary threats in space. In the image, the robotic Shenlong space plane can be seen docked to another satellite that has its solar panels deployed. It's not yet known which satellite that may have been. Shenlong's payload bay doors can also be seen in the photograph, in an open position. Those payload doors may offer clues about what Shenlong is doing on its fourth mission, which launched in February 2026 . China's space agency has stated only that Shenlong helps test technologies that "will pave the way for more convenient and affordable round-trip methods for the peaceful use of space in the future." But observers have seen Shenlong release other objects while in orbit, such as in June 2026, when American space intelligence company LeoLabs reported that itdetected a new object in the vicinity of the space plane. "Following additional observations across our global network and analysis via LeoLabs Delta, we have independently cataloged this object and assessed with high confidence that it was released from the Chinese space plane," LeoLabs stated at the time. "This activity is consistent with sub-satellite deployments conducted by the space plane in previous missions." A similar event happened during Shenlong's third mission , which ended in 2024. On its second mission in 2023, the space plane also released an object and may have conducted what are known as proximity and rendezvous operations, in which two spacecraft maneuver close to one another. It may have been that the spacecraft was releasing unnecessary hardware before landing, however. Like all things military space, few details have been released to the public about Shenlong's operations. The United States, similarly, operates a secretive robotic space plane, the Boeing-built X-37B , and rarely releases concrete details about its capabilities or its missions. In February 2025, the U.S. Space Force released its first photo of the X-37B in space, offering a rare glimpse at the space plane in operation. The photo appeared to show it in a high Earth orbit with what appear to be its payload bay doors open. In 2023, Space Force relea

The photo appeared to show it in a high Earth orbit with what appear to be its payload bay doors open. In 2023, Space Force released its first official painting, depicting an X-37B-like space plane in orbit above Earth, intercepting another satellite . With China and the United States currently jockeying for the lead in what many observers have called a new Space Race , rare glimpses like these images may be a way of militaries and intelligence agencies of teasing capabilities without fully revealing them to the public.

item.title: ‘Elonville’: US residents say Musk’s xAI offered to buy homes if they don’t sue over datacenter noise
item.description: Several Mississippi homes have been purchased near datacenters and one resident said realtor outlined target to buy more than 400 People in a Mississippi neighborhood, many of whom dislike a nearby power plant central to Elon Musk ’s artificial intelligence ambitions, have received a stark offer – to sell their houses to his company and make way. Real estate agents have been going door to door in Southaven, Mississippi, on behalf of xAI, touting a deal to purchase houses as long as the owners agree to not join a lawsuit against the company over the power plant’s noise. (Musk’s AI company officially became SpaceXAI in July and has lately been rebranded as SpaceXSI but to neighbors of the datacenter in Mississippi, it remains xAI.) Continue reading...

item.title: How Google fumbled the frontend with Angular 2
item.description: A cartoon from an ex-Google software engineer, titled “Welcome to Google,” made the rounds a while back. It featured two diverging roads, neither passable. One was the main road, marked as deprecated (“don’t even think about it,” the sign read). The new road, however, was marked as still under construction (“Danger”), and so was unusable as well. That was the no-win choice two million frontend developers faced in 2014, when Google unexpectedly deprecated its popular JavaScript framework, AngularJS, in favor of Angular 2, which had a radically different architecture, a confusing name, no upgrade path, and wasn’t even fully released yet. So, many developers turned the wheel and headed to Reactville or Vuetown instead. How Google botched the Angular upgrade provides timely lessons in how not to update a software package, which former Google Developer Advocate Stephen Fluin outlined in a talk at the All Things Open conference last week. “Uncertainty kills motivation,” said Fluin. “When you're taking away everything [developers] know and love, they're going to feel disheartened.” Fluin is now head of developer relations for Buildkite , but he worked for Google from 2016 to 2021 on the Angular project. “Things were a little bit rough at the time. It was a bit of a death march,” he told the audience. “We had no idea when Angular 2 was going to come out, and the core fundamentals of Angular kept changing.” From AngularJS to Angular 2 Google had good reasons for updating Angular. The AngularJS team had been snatched from Google’s infrastructure division and placed under its ad division, where the software could be more fully exploited. To support operations of that size, Angular needed greater rigor. The original AngularJS was launched in 2009 as a side project of Google engineer Miško Hevery , who wanted to extend HTML. item.dc:creator: Joab Jackson
item.content:encoded: A cartoon from an ex-Google software engineer, titled “Welcome to Google,” made the rounds a while back. It featured two diverging roads, neither passable. One was the main road, marked as deprecated (“don’t even think about it,” the sign read). The new road, however, was marked as still under construction (“Danger”), and so was unusable as well. That was the no-win choice two million frontend developers faced in 2014, when Google unexpectedly deprecated its popular JavaScript framework, AngularJS, in favor of Angular 2, which had a radically different architecture, a confusing name, no upgrade path, and wasn’t even fully released yet. So, many developers turned the wheel and headed to Reactville or Vuetown instead. How Google botched the Angular upgrade provides timely lessons in how not to update a software package, which former Google Developer Advocate Stephen Fluin outlined in a talk at the All Things Open conference last week. “Uncertainty kills motivation,” said Fluin. “When you're taking away everything [developers] know and love, they're going to feel disheartened.” Fluin is now head of developer relations for Buildkite , but he worked for Google from 2016 to 2021 on the Angular project. “Things were a little bit rough at the time. It was a bit of a death march,” he told the audience. “We had no idea when Angular 2 was going to come out, and the core fundamentals of Angular kept changing.” From AngularJS to Angular 2 Google had good reasons for updating Angular. The AngularJS team had been snatched from Google’s infrastructure division and placed under its ad division, where the software could be more fully exploited. To support operations of that size, Angular needed greater rigor. The original AngularJS was launched in 2009 as a side project of Google engineer Miško Hevery , who wanted to extend HTML. Google pulled AngularJS into an internal project because Google developers found it easier to work with than the Java-based Google Web Toolkit ( GWT ). The framework quickly caught on with outside web developers too, who readily understood the angle brackets of HTML (hence the name) and wanted more interactive components. Hevery built AngularJS 1.3 with a traditional controller model, which handled all user input, logic and data transport under the JavaScript $scope object. Angular 2, announced at the ng-europe 2014 conference, was a major shift in architecture. It shifted to a component model, with each HTML template enjoying its own class properties. After a forced, unhappy dalliance with Google's Dart , the team rewrote Angular completely in TypeScript, with no backward compatibility whatsoever. It was a lot to take in, and the introductory talk at ng-europe seemed to spook Angular developers more than inspire them. For each discarded feature, the speakers displayed a graphic of a tombstone (“RIP Controllers”) and played a recording of a church bell tolling in the background. “That talk is still infamous today for what it did to the community,” Fluin said. “All these things that you know and love about AngularJS are gone. They're dead. And nobody knew this was coming.” In general, it was not a good time for software migrations, Fluin noted in his talk. Python was having a rough time migrating from version 2 to 3 , as was the KDE desktop moving from version 4 to version 5. And the rocky transition from GNOME 2 to 3 still loomed in the rearview mirror for many. What's in a name? “If you're trying to bring your developers with you, give them a path. Don't just kill your old thing and then not have a new thing ready,” Fluin advised. Many devs defected to React and Vue.js , two other JavaScript frontend frameworks that also embraced the component model and were already in production. In the 2016 State of JS Survey , React was the most popular frontend framework, with 53 percent of JS devs reporting that they had used it. Angular’s audience was heavily bifurcated; 30 percent still used the classic version while only 13 percent used Angular 2. Ten percent of users adopted the still up-and-coming Vue. Angular 2 was finally released in September 2016, followed by Angular 4 the following March. Version 3 was skipped entirely for no discernable reason. Meanwhile, AngularJS classic, which was not formally retired until the end of 2021, was updated to version 1.5 in the spring of 2016, introducing components. Muddying the waters further was the naming of the frameworks, which confounded many casual observers. Was AngularJS different from Angular 2? And was the “2” part of the Angular name, signaling the complete architectural shift, or its version number? Getting the public to understand the name change turned out to be a major quagmire. Fluin said: “We had to fix public communication guidelines. We had to train experts. We had to fix Google's knowledge graph,” which is Google’s database of facts about the world. “Naming and versioning matter,” he told the audience. “They don't matter in a pure technical sense, but they matter to human beings because it's human beings you're trying to keep up to date with.” It would be easy to blame the Google brass for nearly shipwrecking Angular, but it has been a success at meeting Google’s needs. Today, the component-driven Angular powers Gemini’s user interface, Google Analytics, and countless other Google apps. It is now converging with Google’s internal Wiz high-performance framework, originally designed for the ill-fated Google+ social network. Angular has also settled into a more predictable and user-friendly update pattern. Updates have a routine release cadence, currently twice a year. They dutifully follow semantic versioning guidelines, with major version numbers signifying breaking changes. Google tests each new version of the framework on its own apps before releasing it publicly. Any feature slated for removal is deprecated for a year first. But in retrospect, Google may have been better off giving Angular 2 an entirely different name, even if it meant building up a new user base from scratch. “JavaScript developers loved trying new frameworks. So, pretending to be a new framework might have been better,” Fluin told The Register . ®

item.title: Social media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from?
item.description: AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industry • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here If your social media algorithms have clocked that you’re into video games, something strange will have happened in the past few weeks. Your feed, like mine, will have been full of clips of streamers playing bizarre mashups of popular video games . Skyrim in Minecraft. Halo, except the main character is Mario. Skate 2 in Call of Duty maps. A flood of professional-looking fan-coded game mods that are mildly interesting to look at for 30 seconds, but ultimately inconsequential. Would I download a mod that lets me play Wii Bowling inside a zombie shooter? No, but I am very interested in where they came from. Of course, the answer – or at least, most of the answer – is AI. After a week of researching this (thanks especially to Replay Mode on YouTube for this informative video , which set me down this track) I now understand that these mashup mods are not just AI-generated videos, but AI-assisted coding. Basically, as of a few weeks ago, Anthropic’s Claude has become extremely good at decompiling video game code. Games are written by humans in readable code and then compiled into binary 1s and 0s that the PC or console running it can read; decompiling is the reversal of that process, revealing a game’s source code, which humans can then edit and mess around with for fun. This used to be an extremely laborious process. But now it is not, because humans aren’t doing much of it any more. Continue reading...

item.title: The final ‘Dune: Part Three’ trailer reignites war on Arrakis and leaves us with more questions than answers
item.description: Dune: Part Three 's marketing campaign has been a long and generous one, but Warner Bros. and Legendary Pictures knew an extra push was needed in order to compete with Avengers: Doomsday , as both sci-fi blockbusters will be releasing next to each other at Christmas. In its final trailer, Denis Villeneuve's threequel goes all out. This isn't the first time a Dune: Part Three trailer has left us with more questions than answers , but the in-depth look at the character dynamics and plot beats that await will make longtime fans of Frank Herbert's works raise their eyebrows. Messiah, the second installment in the book series, is a novel of long monologues and very tense conversations. Action has a place in it, but it's a more restrained and quieter book for the most part — one that deals with the consequences of Paul's (now a space dictator) originally well-meaning actions. Of course, the cinematic medium requires a very different language, especially when the main reason why these movies have become blockbuster hits is that Villeneuve has expertly balanced the drama and large-scale action. So, it comes as no surprise that his take on Messiah is looking to bring Herbert's concluding thoughts on Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) to life without sacrificing the grandeur that defined the first two movies. More shocking to readers, of course, is Zendaya's (Chani) much larger role in this finale versus the book, where she was slightly sidelined with a more passive part. Paul's lover walking away from him at the end of Part Two was a major departure, and one that set her up for bigger things in the third entry. Considering how good Zendaya has been in the role so far, we consider this a win... unless Villeneuve completely bungles her arc in the final stretch. Dune: Part Three emerges from the sand of Arrakis on December 18, 2026, only in cinemas. item.title: Eko Hotels at 50: A Defining Moment for African Hospitality on the Global Stage
item.description: The Legacy Gala & Awards night : Fifty Years of Building More Than a Hotel. Fifty Years of Building a Nation’s Hospitality Identity. 2nd of October 2026 was written in the sands of time, because some hotels are built to accommodate history, others are built to make it. For fifty years, Eko Hotels & Suites has done both. Beneath the lights of an extraordinary golden jubilee celebration, one of Africa’s most recognisable hospitality institutions made a statement that extended far beyond the walls of the magnificent Eko Convention Centre . Africa does not lack the capacity to deliver world-class excellence. What it needs are more institutions courageous enough to demonstrate it. The occasion was The Legacy Gala & Awards night, the grand celebration marking fifty years of Eko Hotels & Suites. An evening of African grandeur, international entertainment, cultural pride, distinguished personalities and extraordinary hospitality. But to describe it simply as a glamorous anniversary celebration would be to misunderstand its significance. This was not merely a party, It was fifty years of enterprise taking a bow, Fifty years of memories finding their voices, Fifty years of an institution reminding a continent that excellence is not foreign to Africa a nd for one unforgettable evening, history took attendance. A Hotel Became Part of a Nation’s Story There are buildings that occupy space, and there are institutions that occupy memory, Eko Hotels & Suites belongs to the latter. Across five decades, its corridors have welcomed presidents and policymakers, entrepreneurs and entertainers, diplomats and dreamers, international visitors and generations of Nigerian families. Within its halls, businesses have been negotiated, friendships formed, cultures celebrated, careers launched and milestones immortalized. For many, Eko Hotels is where Lagos welcomes the world, f or others, it is where the world first encounters the warmth, ambition, sophistication and extraordinary possibilities of Lagos. Yet perhaps its greatest achievement is not simply that it has remained standing for fifty years. It is that it has remained RELEVANT. In a world where brands disappear as quickly as trends emerge, longevity is an achievement. But longevity accompanied by reinvention is leadership. Eko Hotels has consistently demonstrated that hospitality must evolve beyond accommodation, It must become an experience, a cultural encounter, a n economic opportunity, a reason to travel and reason to return. Because the greatest hotels do not merely sell rooms. They give destinations a reputation worth travelling for. The Night Africa Wore Her Crown The Legacy Gala & Awards night brought together more than 1,000 distinguished guests, representing an extraordinary convergence of business, government, entertainment, culture and society. item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.content:encoded: The Legacy Gala & Awards night : Fifty Years of Building More Than a Hotel. Fifty Years of Building a Nation’s Hospitality Identity. 2nd of October 2026 was written in the sands of time, because some hotels are built to accommodate history, others are built to make it. For fifty years, Eko Hotels & Suites has done both. Beneath the lights of an extraordinary golden jubilee celebration, one of Africa’s most recognisable hospitality institutions made a statement that extended far beyond the walls of the magnificent Eko Convention Centre . Africa does not lack the capacity to deliver world-class excellence. What it needs are more institutions courageous enough to demonstrate it. The occasion was The Legacy Gala & Awards night, the grand celebration marking fifty years of Eko Hotels & Suites. An evening of African grandeur, international entertainment, cultural pride, distinguished personalities and extraordinary hospitality. But to describe it simply as a glamorous anniversary celebration would be to misunderstand its significance. This was not merely a party, It was fifty years of enterprise taking a bow, Fifty years of memories finding their voices, Fifty years of an institution reminding a continent that excellence is not foreign to Africa a nd for one unforgettable evening, history took attendance. A Hotel Became Part of a Nation’s Story There are buildings that occupy space, and there are institutions that occupy memory, Eko Hotels & Suites belongs to the latter. Across five decades, its corridors have welcomed presidents and policymakers, entrepreneurs and entertainers, diplomats and dreamers, international visitors and generations of Nigerian families. Within its halls, businesses have been negotiated, friendships formed, cultures celebrated, careers launched and milestones immortalized. For many, Eko Hotels is where Lagos welcomes the world, f or others, it is where the world first encounters the warmth, ambition, sophistication and extraordinary possibilities of Lagos. Yet perhaps its greatest achievement is not simply that it has remained standing for fifty years. It is that it has remained RELEVANT. In a world where brands disappear as quickly as trends emerge, longevity is an achievement. But longevity accompanied by reinvention is leadership. Eko Hotels has consistently demonstrated that hospitality must evolve beyond accommodation, It must become an experience, a cultural encounter, a n economic opportunity, a reason to travel and reason to return. Because the greatest hotels do not merely sell rooms. They give destinations a reputation worth travelling for. The Night Africa Wore Her Crown The Legacy Gala & Awards night brought together more than 1,000 distinguished guests, representing an extraordinary convergence of business, government, entertainment, culture and society. Among the dignitaries were Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu , Deputy Governor Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat , prominent business leaders, industry executives, celebrities and long-standing friends of the institution. It was a gathering that reflected not simply the prestige of a hotel, but the depth of relationships cultivated across generations. The evening’s entertainment brought together internationally celebrated musician Wyclef Jean and Nigerian highlife sensation Flavour , creating a memorable meeting of African and Caribbean musical heritage. Music, fashion, theatrical expression and celebration converged in a spectacle befitting the occasion. Yet, beyond the performances lay a more compelling message. African creativity is not a decorative addition to hospitality. It is one of it’s greatest competitive advantages. Africa’s music travels the world, African fashion influences global runways, African cuisine carries the memory of generations, African storytelling continues to captivate audiences far beyond our borders and, many started on Eko Hotels grounds. The question is no longer whether Africa possesses what the world desires, t he question is whether we are sufficiently intentional about converting these cultural assets into sustainable industries, jobs, investments and compelling destination experiences. At The Gala, Eko Hotels offered its own answer. Africa need not borrow another continent’s identity to earn the world’s admiration. She need only invest boldly enough in her own. There is, however, another story that deserves equal billing. It is the story of the people, n ot the famous faces photographed beneath the lights, n ot the glittering personalities whose arrival commands applause b ut the extraordinary men and women whose daily dedication has sustained Eko Hotels for half a century. The housekeepers who prepare rooms with meticulous care, t he waiters who understand that genuine service is an act of dignity, t he engineers who keep an enormous hospitality operation functioning, the security personnel who protect its people and promises, t he gardeners, technicians, stewards, reservation officers, accountants, sales professionals, event planners, administrative teams and countless others whose contributions rarely make newspaper headlines. These are the custodians of the brand. The quiet architects of its reputation and t he human infrastructure behind its commercial success. For fifty years, generations of employees have given their skills, energy, creativity and commitment to an institution that has become part of Nigeria’s hospitality heritage. Their stories may not always appear in annual reports, but their fingerprints are everywhere. A hotel may be built with concrete, steel and capital. But a legacy is built with people who choose, every day, to care. The Chairman, Christopher Chagoury boldly said in an interview. Perhaps, this is one of the most important lessons of Eko Hotels at fifty: buildings can be replicated, interiors redesigned and technology acquired, but a culture of excellence must be nurtured and that culture is ultimately human. The Leadership understands the weight of the legacy. Behind every enduring institution is a succession of decisions, investments, sacrifices and moments when leadership chooses long-term value over immediate convenience. The golden jubilee provided an opportunity to recognize the vision and stewardship that have guided Eko Hotels through five decades. Under the leadership of their Managing Director, Ghassan Faddoul , General Manager Danny Kioupouroglou and the wider executive management team, the institution continues to strengthen it’s position as a defining hospitality destination. Their collective responsibility extends beyond protecting a celebrated past, to redesigning a future, our past will be proud of, long after we are gone. It is to ensure that the institution remains competitive, innovative and relevant to future generations. The true measure of leadership, after all, is not simply what it achieves during its tenure, i t is what remains valuable long after that tenure has ended. Legacy is not the applause we receive while we are present. It is the relevance of what we build when we are no longer in the room. Fifty years of Eko Hotels is therefore not merely a tribute to endurance, i t is a testament to institutional stewardship. From Hospitality To Destination Economics Perhaps the most consequential chapter in Eko Hotels’ evolution is it’s expanding role in connecting hospitality with tourism, culture, entertainment and the creative economy. Through initiatives such as Tropical Christmas Wonderland, Theatre @ Eko Hotels, Hakuna Matata Theme Park and other destination experiences, the institution has increasingly demonstrated how hospitality infrastructure can become a platform for cultural production and economic participation. These initiatives represent a larger philosophy: a hotel should not wait for tourism demand to arrive. It can actively help create the reasons people travel. item.title: Microsoft faces potential vote: Shareholders curious about its plans to tackle emissions
item.description: Trillium Asset Management wants Microsoft to explain how it will meet its 2030 greenhouse gas (GHG) emission targets, and is backing a shareholder proposal to request this information at the firm’s next shareholder meeting. The cloud and software biz set itself lofty environmental goals back in 2020 , aiming to be become "carbon-negative" by 2030, and to have removed the equivalent of all the carbon it has ever emitted by 2050. But since the start of the decade, an explosion in AI development and demand for ever more complex models has seen a boom in demand for high-performance compute infrastructure and a construction wave to deliver new datacenters to house it all in. Microsoft is one of the firms to profit from this huge demand, with its cloud division making $214.4 billion in revenue for the fiscal year 2026 ended June 30, a 27 percent year-on-year increase. This has also caused Microsoft’s emissions to head in the wrong direction, with figures from the company’s most recent Environmental Sustainability Report showing that these have increased from 13 million tons of CO 2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million tons in 2025. However, Microsoft estimates that without the carbon reduction initiatives it has already put in place, emissions would now be much higher, somewhere near 34 million tons. The increase is largely accounted for by indirect emissions (Scope 3) from the construction and provisioning of datacenters to meet that demand for cloud services and AI training. But as The Register pointed out, 2025 saw a growing contribution from Scope 2, due to generation of energy the company purchased. This represents 13 percent of total emissions – up from 2 percent in 2024. Now Trillium Asset Management, financial advisors specializing in sustainable and responsible investing, is urging Microsoft shareholders to vote for Proposal 4 during their annual meeting scheduled for December 8. In an SEC filing , the proposal asks Microsoft to disclose additional information illustrating how it will manage climate commitments. This disclosure should go beyond existing disclosures, at reasonable cost, omitting proprietary information, and be made annually. The proposal notes that when Microsoft first announced its carbon negative goal, it said progress required "not just a bold goal but a detailed plan," and that transparency was one of the guiding principles for this climate plan. It states that emissions are now 62 percent above the 2020 baseline, and simply asks Microsoft to apply the principles it articulated in 2020; show the plan, be candid about the math, and explain how it will adapt. In the filing, Trillium warns that falling short of its climate targets may create risk to Microsoft’s credibility, which can influence investor trust. item.content:encoded: Trillium Asset Management wants Microsoft to explain how it will meet its 2030 greenhouse gas (GHG) emission targets, and is backing a shareholder proposal to request this information at the firm’s next shareholder meeting. The cloud and software biz set itself lofty environmental goals back in 2020 , aiming to be become "carbon-negative" by 2030, and to have removed the equivalent of all the carbon it has ever emitted by 2050. But since the start of the decade, an explosion in AI development and demand for ever more complex models has seen a boom in demand for high-performance compute infrastructure and a construction wave to deliver new datacenters to house it all in. Microsoft is one of the firms to profit from this huge demand, with its cloud division making $214.4 billion in revenue for the fiscal year 2026 ended June 30, a 27 percent year-on-year increase. This has also caused Microsoft’s emissions to head in the wrong direction, with figures from the company’s most recent Environmental Sustainability Report showing that these have increased from 13 million tons of CO 2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million tons in 2025. However, Microsoft estimates that without the carbon reduction initiatives it has already put in place, emissions would now be much higher, somewhere near 34 million tons. The increase is largely accounted for by indirect emissions (Scope 3) from the construction and provisioning of datacenters to meet that demand for cloud services and AI training. But as The Register pointed out, 2025 saw a growing contribution from Scope 2, due to generation of energy the company purchased. This represents 13 percent of total emissions – up from 2 percent in 2024. Now Trillium Asset Management, financial advisors specializing in sustainable and responsible investing, is urging Microsoft shareholders to vote for Proposal 4 during their annual meeting scheduled for December 8. In an SEC filing , the proposal asks Microsoft to disclose additional information illustrating how it will manage climate commitments. This disclosure should go beyond existing disclosures, at reasonable cost, omitting proprietary information, and be made annually. The proposal notes that when Microsoft first announced its carbon negative goal, it said progress required "not just a bold goal but a detailed plan," and that transparency was one of the guiding principles for this climate plan. It states that emissions are now 62 percent above the 2020 baseline, and simply asks Microsoft to apply the principles it articulated in 2020; show the plan, be candid about the math, and explain how it will adapt. In the filing, Trillium warns that falling short of its climate targets may create risk to Microsoft’s credibility, which can influence investor trust. If Microsoft is in danger of failing to meet its 2030 commitments, it could suffer reputational harm, and the filing claims it is already the subject of legal action by investors alleging insufficient disclosure of its AI and cloud spending. On the flip side, it says that disclosure of a climate transition plan will likely prove valuable to large institutional investors who view climate change as a systemic risk to future economic growth. We asked Microsoft for comment, but it already recommended in another SEC filing that shareholders vote against the proposal, arguing it fails to show that Microsoft’s existing disclosures are insufficient for investors to assess its climate-related strategy and performance. Instead, the firm says that the proposal requests a collection of new disclosures that go beyond not just legal and regulatory requirements, but also established voluntary climate-reporting frameworks. The proposal seeks hypothetical scenarios, contingency plans and other forward-looking information that is inherently uncertain and subject to change, Microsoft states, saying it will remain focused on its Sustainability Report and other environmental reporting while meeting any new disclosure mandates that may arise globally. ®

item.title: Satellites watch an escaping Antarctic iceberg | Space photo of the day for Oct. 28, 2026
item.description: null Iceberg A-81 escaping the Weddell Sea and drifting near the edge of South Georgia's underwater shelf. The image was captured on Oct. 20, 2026. (Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison) An iceberg has quickly escaped from the Weddell Sea in Antarctica, on its way to an icy new destination. What is it? As captured by a satellite in orbit, the Antarctic iceberg A-81 has quite quickly (for an iceberg) parted ways from its icy home, breaking off to drift toward a shallow underwater shelf in Georgia. The 600-square-mile (1,550-square-kilometer) iceberg first broke off from the Brunt Ice Shelf in January of 2023. Now, generally speaking, giant icebergs don't travel that fast. But In just three years, this massive iceberg has traveled 1,400 miles (2,300 kilometers) north of the Brunt Ice Shelf. For an iceberg, that's really fast. Over this time period, the iceberg drifted through the Weddell Sea in Antarctica's Southern Ocean before reaching the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula, floating further into the Scotia Sea and then finally now reaching the edge of a remote island in South Georgia. In this satellite snapshot captured on Oct. 20, 2026, we can see the iceberg in its current location near an underwater shelf off the coast of South Georgia. While it isn't abnormal for icebergs like A-81 to break off from larger ice shelves, Brunt has recently had multiple large icebergs break off one quickly after the other, according to a statement from NASA . Why is it incredible? This image was captured by the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer), an instrument on board NASA's Terra satellite. Earth -observing satellites like Terra keep a close eye on changes on our home planet. In addition to this image, observations from Terra have showed how the iceberg has traveled over the last few years. With satellites like Terra, scientists can keep a close eye on these changes in Antarctic ice, which is becoming increasingly important as climate change continues to progress across the globe, affecting everything from Arctic ice to sea levels rising, worsening natural disasters and more.

item.title: Max Dowman’s Fleetwood fracas leaves him, Arsenal and Arteta red-faced
item.description: Teenager was maybe harshly sent off in the Carabao Cup tie but his reaction was a mistake he will learn from, while his manager might also have regrets Mikel Arteta’s reaction said it all. As Max Dowman trudged towards the touchline after becoming the youngest player sent off in a League Cup match at 16 years and 300 days, the Arsenal manager could not help himself. Arms folded across his chest like an angry father who has caught his teenage son sneaking in after midnight, Arteta leaned over and aimed a few choice words in Dowman’s direction before the forward headed sheepishly down the tunnel. What he said remains unknown, although that hasn’t stopped the amateur lip-readers speculating on social media. “Get in the changing room. Now,” appears the most likely guess. Continue reading...

item.title: China's spaceplane bears striking resemblance to America's X-37B
item.description: China's secretive spaceplane has been spotted in orbit by a US commercial satellite, according to the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) The DIA's report [PDF] warns of developments by China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea that allegedly threaten space security, at least from a US perspective. Most of the report details systems still under development, but one image on page 53 stands out: China's spaceplane, snapped in orbit in 2024 by Maxar Technologies. The image has been seen before; a low-resolution snap from an industry symposium was shared by Bluesky user @dutchspace almost two years ago. However, the higher-resolution image in the DIA report shows more detail. The spaceplane also bears a distinct resemblance to the US Space Force's X-37B. The uncrewed X-37 began as a NASA project in 1999 before the US Department of Defense took over. After several atmospheric tests with an X-37A variant, the X-37B was launched in 2010. The reusable spaceplane can spend years in orbit, conducting classified activities. So far, it has launched eight times. According to the DIA's report, China's first spaceplane mission launched in 2020 and remained in orbit for two days. A second, launched in 2022, spent 276 days in orbit, and a third, launched in December 2023, spent 268 days in oribt. The last two missions appeared to include approach and rendezvous tests of objects in orbit. Russia, memorably, had a spaceplane in the ill-fated Buran, which bore an uncanny resemblance to the US Space Shuttle (although the two were very different beasts from a technical perspective – not least, Buran's orbiter did not carry the engines used to launch it to space). However, according to the DIA's report, Russia "has made little progress since." The US recently confirmed that it has weapons in space, and it would be naive not to assume rivals would have their own, whether kinetic or some form of jamming technology. Earlier this month, Russia's Kosmos-2612 sidled up to the US ICEYE-X36 satellite before retreating. It's unclear whether the intention was an entirely innocent look at a fellow spacecraft or a bit of saber-rattling; it certainly worried US lawmakers . ®

item.title: Yinka Ogunbiyi Shows HaloBraid’s Automated Hair-Braiding Technology in New Demo
item.description: Harvard graduate Yinka Ogunbiyi, creator of the automated HaloBraid device engineered to complete braids up to five times faster. What if you could get your braids done in a fraction of the usual time and still leave the salon with the style you wanted? A new demonstration of HaloBraid, the automated braiding device created by Nigerian-American engineer and Harvard graduate Yinka Ogunbiyi , gives us a closer look at how that could work. Designed to help professional hairdressers braid hair up to five times faster while reducing the physical strain that comes with hours of styling, HaloBraid is now being demonstrated in action. And the interesting part is that the machine doesn’t do everything. The stylist still plays an important role in the process. Here’s how it works. The stylist sections the hair, applies the necessary products and starts the braid by hand before feeding it into the device. HaloBraid then handles the repetitive weaving along the length of the hair, while the stylist returns to finish and seal the ends. This means the machine takes care of a time-consuming part of the process, with the stylist still responsible for creating the final hairstyle. For Yinka, the idea behind HaloBraid comes from a very personal experience. Sharing the story behind the invention, she said: My braid story starts at age four, sitting between my mum’s legs as she braided my hair for the first time. Since then, I’ve spent thousands of hours getting my hair braided — and heard the same story from stylists and clients again and again: braiding is beautiful, but it takes too much time and too much strain. As a biomechanical engineer, I knew there had to be a better way, so we built HaloBraid with stylists from the beginning, bringing together inventors, designers, and builders behind some of the world’s most loved hair and beauty products. HaloBraid was built for my mum, my stylists, my aunties, and people around the world who know what it means to spend hours in the chair. The company has also secured $7 million in seed funding, with the investment round led by Seven Seven Six, the venture capital firm founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian , who is married to tennis champion Serena Williams . With the newly shared demonstration, HaloBraid is showing how its technology works alongside professional stylists, combining hand-braiding techniques with automated weaving to reduce the time and physical effort involved in protective hairstyling. The post Yinka Ogunbiyi Shows HaloBraid’s Automated Hair-Braiding Technology in New Demo appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .
