item.title: Yemi Alade Is Counting Cash and Serving Looks in “Alhaja” Video
item.description: Yemi Alade wears a gold-embroidered black abaya in her “Alhaja” music video. We love how Yemi Alade gives us something new to talk about with each music video. If she isn’t channelling a photographer who could give Don Jazzy a run for his money, she’s stepping into the shoes of an Alhaja who clearly has money to spend, and she’s having a great time doing it. In the official music video for “Alhaja”, a standout track from her latest album, It’s Yemi Alade , the Afropop star leans into rich cultural aesthetics, striking outfits and scenes that feel like a celebration of success. Directed by Clarence Peters , the video plays with neon lighting, atmospheric torchlight and a cast that knows how to make an entrance. Yemi Alade holds a stack of cash in a scene from her “Alhaja” music video. Yemi has a wardrobe change for every mood, too. In one scene, she appears in a traditional red outfit, complete with a structured headwrap and layers of coral beads. Then comes a black-and-gold embroidered abaya, paired with bold gold hand jewellery and ornate rings. She’s giving us an Alhaja who knows exactly what she’s worth, and the styling makes sure we don’t miss it. Yemi Alade holds a stack of cash in a scene from her “Alhaja” music video. The details around her are just as fun. Vintage cars set the scene, traditional drums bring in the cultural touches, and cast members count cash beneath warm lanterns. It all adds to the video’s celebration of identity, prosperity and personal achievement, with Yemi right at the centre of it. With “Alhaja”, Yemi Alade gives us another music video with a distinct visual world, memorable styling and plenty of personality. And really, would we expect anything less? item.title: What is The Hidden Cost of Nigerian Women’s Unpaid Labour?
item.description: Mother and children preparing food in a bright, cosy kitchen setting. Credit: RDNE Stock Project/Pexels. Fadekemi was six when she first felt the sting of splattered hot oil on her skin. She recalls her mother’s stern voice instructing her on how to make stew the way her father liked it. Fifty-one years and thousands of stew pots later, Fadekemi still wonders if that’s all she was made to do. In different parts of Nigeria today, there are millions of women like Fadekemi, each spending at least 5 hours daily on unpaid care and domestic work. Although Nigerians rarely pay women for care and domestic duties, research shows that it is real work with an annual economic value of up to $111 billion . How Women Carry Nigeria’s Unpaid Labour According to the Nigeria Time Use Survey (NTUS) 2024 report, the average Nigerian woman spends 21% of her day on unpaid domestic and care work ; this equals 5 extra hours, while men spend just one hour on unpaid work. This means that after spending 8 hours at work, she spends another 5 hours doing childcare and household work, making it a double shift. Yet when you look at the economic drivers of Nigeria’s economy, her time or work does not count; it is seen as a woman’s work. This inequality is seen as invisible labour. We see it show up in different phases of women’s lives, yet we still miss how heavy an unequal burden this is. Right from when a girl is 13, she becomes an unpaid labourer, doing domestic chores, taking care of siblings, yet these contributions are seen as nothing to Nigeria’s GDP. For Fadekemi, this unpaid labour started at six, continued into her teenage years, where she became a caregiver for her siblings, extended into motherhood, and now, as a grandmother, she continues to be a caregiver for her grandchildren because even traditions like Omugwo exclude men from care duties. Behind those hours of unpaid labour is a missed opportunity for the country’s GDP growth. What Happens When Care Is Shared? In a 2026 study published in BMC Paediatrics, over 64% of women said they were the primary caregivers of their newborn children. In some cases, this is a result of traditional belief systems that reinforce gender roles and assign domestic duties to women. In other cases, it is a systemic failure caused by policies that reinforce gender inequality. In Nigeria, for example, mothers are entitled to maternity leave with 50% pay, while only fathers in the civil service are entitled to 14 days of paternity leave. So what happens to private sector fathers? The national policy designs them to be absent fathers from day one and reinforces the narrative that their sole role is to be a provider and presence doesn’t matter. Experts have highlighted that cutting a new mother’s salary by 50% while excluding most fathers from paid leave reinforces the belief that a man’s primary duty is to be a financial provider and makes it harder for them to be present. And when that happens, care once again becomes the woman’s job.

So what happens to private sector fathers? The national policy designs them to be absent fathers from day one and reinforces the narrative that their sole role is to be a provider and presence doesn’t matter. And when that happens, care once again becomes the woman’s job. According to Nigeria’s proposed National Care Policy, when care duties are shared, the entire country benefits. Care moves from an unpaid, largely invisible responsibility to a thriving economic sector that creates jobs, supports businesses, strengthens national productivity, and enables millions of women to participate more fully in the labour market. Recognising the value of care work drives employment of 1.7 million mothers and could add $111 billion to the economy, 8 times more than the oil sector. This invisible labour has a price tag, and even though it appears that Nigerian women are the only ones who bear the cost, the entire country pays for it. When one segment of the population is unable to fully participate in the labour market, growth stalls for everyone. If you’d like to provide input on the draft of the National Care Policy, please do so at nigeriacarepolicy.org . item.title: 25 and Golden! Dede Ashiogwu Celebrates in a Gorgeous Butter-Yellow Two-Piece
item.description: Dede celebrates her 25th birthday in a draped butter yellow chiffon set. Butter yellow on melanin is already a winning combination, but Big Brother Naija Season 10 star Dede is taking it somewhere much more fabulous. Celebrating her birthday on 23 October 2026, the content creator, whose full name is Ashiogwu Precious , has gifted us a set of Renaissance-inspired portraits that could easily pass for paintings in a grand old gallery. And the outfit at the centre of it all? A custom butter-yellow two-piece that makes a very good case for giving this pretty shade a spot in your wardrobe. Dede wears a custom butter yellow gathering bandeau top and low-rise train skirt by Precious Phillips. Dede handled the creative direction herself, working with designer Precious Phillips on a gathered bandeau top and a low-rise maxi skirt that follows her figure before spilling into a floor-sweeping train. The colour is gorgeous against her skin, and that dramatic silhouette gives the look a regal, almost otherworldly quality without feeling stuck in another century. Of course, the beauty look had to keep up. Yellow feathers frame her eyes, a thick side-braided ponytail sweeps through her hair, and her glowing makeup ties everything together. Add a golden hand mirror and a moody, canvas-style backdrop, and you have birthday portraits that look as though they were dreamed up in an artist’s studio. Dede poses with a golden handheld mirror in her self-styled Renaissance birthday shoot. The best part is that you don’t need a Renaissance-inspired photoshoot to take a little inspiration from Dede. Butter yellow works beautifully in flowing chiffon, sheer mesh and other lightweight fabrics, whether you’re dressing for a birthday dinner or simply want to try something new. Gold jewellery complements the shade beautifully, while pared-back accessories give statement silhouettes and playful eye makeup room to shine. Dede complements her birthday look with soft yellow feather eye flourishes and gold leaf drop earrings. Dede may have given butter yellow the full birthday-treatment treatment, but the takeaway is simple: this shade deserves a place in your fashion rotation. Ashiogwu Precious (Dede) marks her 25th birthday in a butter yellow two-piece set by Precious Phillips. Ashiogwu Precious (Dede) seated beside warm floral accents in her custom Precious Phillips birthday outfit. *** Photo Credit: Ashiogwu Precious/Instagram The post 25 and Golden! item.content:encoded: Dede celebrates her 25th birthday in a draped butter yellow chiffon set. Butter yellow on melanin is already a winning combination, but Big Brother Naija Season 10 star Dede is taking it somewhere much more fabulous. Celebrating her birthday on 23 October 2026, the content creator, whose full name is Ashiogwu Precious , has gifted us a set of Renaissance-inspired portraits that could easily pass for paintings in a grand old gallery. And the outfit at the centre of it all? A custom butter-yellow two-piece that makes a very good case for giving this pretty shade a spot in your wardrobe. Dede wears a custom butter yellow gathering bandeau top and low-rise train skirt by Precious Phillips. Dede handled the creative direction herself, working with designer Precious Phillips on a gathered bandeau top and a low-rise maxi skirt that follows her figure before spilling into a floor-sweeping train. The colour is gorgeous against her skin, and that dramatic silhouette gives the look a regal, almost otherworldly quality without feeling stuck in another century. Of course, the beauty look had to keep up. Yellow feathers frame her eyes, a thick side-braided ponytail sweeps through her hair, and her glowing makeup ties everything together. Add a golden hand mirror and a moody, canvas-style backdrop, and you have birthday portraits that look as though they were dreamed up in an artist’s studio. Dede poses with a golden handheld mirror in her self-styled Renaissance birthday shoot. The best part is that you don’t need a Renaissance-inspired photoshoot to take a little inspiration from Dede. Butter yellow works beautifully in flowing chiffon, sheer mesh and other lightweight fabrics, whether you’re dressing for a birthday dinner or simply want to try something new. Gold jewellery complements the shade beautifully, while pared-back accessories give statement silhouettes and playful eye makeup room to shine. Dede complements her birthday look with soft yellow feather eye flourishes and gold leaf drop earrings. Dede may have given butter yellow the full birthday-treatment treatment, but the takeaway is simple: this shade deserves a place in your fashion rotation. item.title: Janelle Monáe Spreads Her Fashion Wings in a Sculptural Robert Wun Gown
item.description: Janelle Monáe wears a custom blue sequined Robert Wun gown at the 2026 Academy Museum Gala. Butterfly in a dress? Janelle Monáe says bring it on! We’ve seen butterflies inspire jewellery, hair accessories and even prints on dresses, but a giant, three-dimensional butterfly forming the bodice of a gown? Now that’s something worth talking about. And who better to wear it than the acclaimed singer, songwriter, and actress Janelle Monáe, who has never been afraid to have a little fun with fashion? For the 6th Annual Academy Museum Gala, held on 17 October 2026 in Los Angeles, the singer and actress known for her memorable roles in Hidden Figures , Moonlight , and Glass Onion , stepped onto the red carpet in a Robert Wun creation that looked like a butterfly had spread its wings right across her chest. The gown, from the designer’s Fall 2026 Couture collection, featured a fitted mermaid silhouette covered in sequins that moved from rich blue to black. But the real attraction was that enormous three-dimensional butterfly bodice, with its wings extending across her upper body. Janelle Monáe attends the 2026 Academy Museum Gala in a custom Robert Wun mermaid dress. And Janelle wasn’t about to let the butterfly theme end with the dress. Styled by Alexandra Mandelkorn , she paired the gown with sheer opera-length gloves, metallic blue stiletto nails and a soft pixie cut finished with a little butterfly hair clip. Even the smallest details played along with the look, without competing with that spectacular bodice. Janelle Monáe in custom Robert Wun Couture at the 6th Annual Academy Museum Gala. Now, if you’re wondering how to borrow a little inspiration from this look without wearing an enormous butterfly to your next event, there’s something to learn from Janelle’s styling. When your outfit already has a striking feature, you can afford to keep everything else simple. Skip the heavy necklaces, let the shape of the dress do its thing and choose accessories that complement its colours. And those shades of blue are worth experimenting with, too. Cobalt, navy and other rich jewel tones can look beautiful together, especially when you carry a little of the colour into your makeup or accessories. Janelle’s look might be straight from the couture runway, but the styling ideas are ones you can have fun with in your own wardrobe. Janelle Monáe showcases the three-dimensional butterfly bodice of her Robert Wun Fall 2026 Couture gown. Janelle Monáe wearing blue eye makeup and metallic nails to match her Robert Wun butterfly gown. *** Photo Credit: Janelle Monáe/Instagram The post Janelle Monáe Spreads Her Fashion Wings in a Sculptural Robert Wun Gown appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: Tanqueray Lagos Cocktail Week: Tanqueray Brings Citrus Creativity To The Lagos Cocktail Week
item.description: Tanqueray brought its signature spirit of creativity and craftsmanship to Lagos Cocktail Week 2026 , inviting consumers to experience cocktail culture in a fresh and immersive way. At the heart of the experience was a vibrant citrus-inspired cocktail journey that encouraged guests to explore flavour, creativity, and personal expression. Consumers had the opportunity to craft their own Tanqueray cocktails, experimenting with a variety of garnishes, mixers, and flavour combinations to create serves tailored to their individual tastes. From bright citrus notes to bold flavour pairings, the experience celebrated the artistry behind great cocktails while making mixology approachable, engaging, and memorable. Beyond enjoying expertly crafted serves, guests were invited to personalize their experience by creating bespoke cocktail recipe cards featuring their chosen ingredients and serves. These take-home keepsakes allowed consumers to recreate their favourite Tanqueray cocktails long after the event had ended. Throughout Lagos Cocktail Week, the Tanqueray booth became a destination for cocktail enthusiasts looking to discover new flavour profiles, learn more about the craft of mixology, and connect with fellow cocktail lovers in a vibrant and stylish setting. The partnership underscored Tanqueray’s commitment to championing premium cocktail culture in Nigeria while creating memorable experiences that bring people together through exceptional cocktails and meaningful moments. Drink Responsibly. Not for persons under the legal purchase age. item.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
item.description: An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. Continue reading...

item.title: Adekunle Gold Foundation and PESA Launch ‘We Are Not Done’ Sickle Cell Impact Initiative
item.description: The Adekunle Gold Foundation (AG Foundation), in partnership with Pesa , has launched We’re Not Done: AG Foundation Sickle Cell Impact Initiative , a new programme designed to strengthen organisations providing critical support to people living with sickle cell disease. Launching with a $20,000 commitment from Pesa , the initiative will provide funding to selected sickle cell organisations, helping them expand their work across healthcare access, patient support, education, awareness and advocacy. For its inaugural cycle, We’re Not Done will support AG Foundation’s work alongside the following 4 beneficiaries, Sickle Cell Advocacy Management Initiative (NIGERIA), Not Just You (CANADA), Sickle Life (GHANA), It Takes A Village (UK) recognizing the important work each organisation is already doing within the sickle cell community. The funding will enable the organisations to strengthen existing programmes, expand their reach and deepen their impact. For A dekunle Gold, who has lived openly with sickle cell disease and used his platform to advocate for the community, We’re Not Done represents a commitment to supporting the organisations already doing vital work on the ground. “ We’re Not Done is about turning awareness into action. There are incredible organisations working every day to improve the lives of people living with sickle cell, and together with Pesa, we want to give them more resources to do that work and reach even more people.” Adekunle Gold said. Pesa joins the initiative as its programme partner , supporting both the launch and first cycle of impact. “ Sickle cell affects many people in the Nigerian and wider Black communities we serve. These are our friends, colleagues, and loved ones. Adekunle Gold has shown how a personal connection to an issue can become a force for meaningful change, and we’re proud to support the launch of We’re Not Done , an initiative dedicated to raising awareness and supporting the sickle cell community. Through our partnership with the AG Foundation and the other participating foundations, we hope to go beyond awareness and contribute to meaningful, tangible support for individuals and families affected by sickle cell, ” said Tosin Olaniyi (Head, Global Growth & Marketing, Pesa) Through We’re Not Done , AG Foundation, with the support of Pesa, aims to build a platform that combines funding, advocacy and visibility to strengthen the wider sickle cell ecosystem and create measurable, lasting impact. Because for the sickle cell community, we’re not done. About Adekunle Gold Foundation Adekunle Gold Foundation was founded in 2023 by singer/songwriter Adekunle Gold. The foundation is committed to improving the lives of those living with sickle cell disease through healthcare access, advocacy, and awareness. item.title: Macro Photographer, Dara Ojo, Shares Stories Behind Some of His Photographs
item.description: Following our feature on Dara Ojo , a Nigerian macro photographer on his journey into photography and his forthcoming book, we invited him to share stories behind three of his selected photographs. Dara grew up in Nigeria and is currently based in Canada, but his photography journey began in China during the COVID-19 pandemic. You can read Dara’s story here while reading the stories behind his selected photographs. Hello Dara, we hope you’re well. Thank you for sharing your journey with us. You have selected three photographs to tell us the stories behind. Why these photos? Thank you for having me. The photos I selected are Planthopper Nymph, Silkworm Moth and Leafhopper Infected by Metarhizium Fungus. I selected them because they all have something in common: Costa Rica. They were all shot in Costa Rica. Let me share the story behind each, and you will get a proper picture. Silkworm Moth Silkworm Moth by Nigerian macro photographer Dara Ojo. I photographed this beautiful silkworm moth in Costa Rica while filming the PBS documentary Bugs That Rule the World . What I love about moths is how often people underestimate them. Many assume they’re dull, but when you get close enough, you discover incredible colours, patterns and textures. This particular moth was a wonderful example of that hidden beauty. Being able to document creatures like this while working on a wildlife documentary was a special experience, and it’s a reminder of how much of nature’s beauty we overlook simply because we don’t stop to look closely. Leafhopper Infected by Metarhizium Fungus Leafhopper overtaken by Fungi. Photo by Dara Ojo. This is probably one of the strangest things I’ve photographed in nature. I came across this leafhopper in Costa Rica, and a parasitic fungus called Metarhizium had completely overtaken its body . The fungus infects insects, grows inside their bodies and eventually kills them. Under suitable conditions, it then grows out of the insect’s body and produces spores that can infect other insects. It’s fascinating and a little unsettling. If you’ve watched The Last of Us , you’ll probably recognise the inspiration behind the show’s fictional fungal infection, although the fungi involved are different. What makes this photograph so remarkable to me is that it almost looks like something from a science fiction movie, yet it’s a real interaction happening in nature. Sometimes, the natural world is far stranger than anything we could imagine. Planthopper Nymph Planthopper nymph by Nigerian macro photographer Dara Ojo. This is one of the trickiest little creatures I’ve ever photographed. It’s a planthopper nymph, a tiny insect with beautiful, waxy strands extending from the back of its body. Finding one is difficult enough because they’re incredibly small, but getting a good photograph is another challenge entirely. This is one of the trickiest little creatures I’ve ever photographed. It’s a planthopper nymph, a tiny insect with beautiful, waxy strands extending from the back of its body. Finding one is difficult enough because they’re incredibly small, but getting a good photograph is another challenge entirely. They have a habit of turning away whenever you try to photograph them, almost as though they’re deliberately avoiding the camera. You have to be patient and strategic with your movements because one wrong move and they’re gone. It took quite a bit of persistence, but moments like this are exactly why I love macro photography. Thank you for sharing these stories with us, Dara Thank you again for having me. _ Dara Ojo’s Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem will be published on November 10, 2026, and will be available internationally. It will have public book launches in Edmonton on November 25 and Toronto on December 2, with additional events being explored for New York in March 2027 and Vancouver in April 2027. item.title: Veteran Nollywood Actor Francis Duru Passes Away at 57 | Read Family Statement
item.description: Veteran Nollywood actor Francis Duru has passed away at the age of 57. Photo Credit: Francis Duru/Instagram The Nigerian film industry has been thrown into mourning following the sad passing of veteran Nollywood actor, director,and academic, Francis Duru . The respected movie star passed away at the age of 57 following a brief illness, leaving behind a incredible legacy that spans over three decades of memorable performances across television and cinema. Sharing the heartbreaking news with fans and well-wishers on his official Instagram page, his family released a moving statement: We, the family of Francis Duru, regret to announce his passing following a brief illness. We appreciate your prayers, love, and understanding. May his soul rest in perfect peace. Amen. A true pioneer of modern Nollywood, Francis Duru made his screen debut back in 1989 in the feature Missing Mark , before shooting to nationwide fame for his unforgettable portrayal of Ahanna in Amaka Igwe ’s 1995 classic Rattlesnake . Over the years, he cemented his status as a household name with stellar roles in acclaimed movies such as Blood Money , Mama Sunday , Total Control , Home in Exile , Mboputa , and Stigma . Beyond his stellar career in front of the camera, Duru was a dedicated academic holding a degree in Theatre Arts from the University of Port Harcourt, and a passionate advocate who served as a United Nations Ambassador of Peace and as interim President of the Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN). Francis Duru is survived by his loving wife, Adokiye Duru , whom he married in 2003, and their children The post Veteran Nollywood Actor Francis Duru Passes Away at 57 | Read Family Statement appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Naomi Ackie Was Anything but Basic in Sculptural Schiaparelli at Paris Fashion Week
item.description: Naomi Ackie Naomi Ackie has been delivering some serious fashion moments lately, and her appearance at the Schiaparelli show during Paris Fashion Week is another one for the books. The British-Grenadian actress wore a striking black, single-sleeved gown that perfectly captured the house’s surrealist sensibility. Thousands of finely worked pleats created an almost liquid effect, hugging her figure before falling into a dramatic thigh-high slit. But what really makes this look special is the exaggerated sleeve, which gives the otherwise sleek silhouette an architectural quality. Naomi has worn the brand a few times, and we love how she always embraces the brand’s aesthetic without letting it overwhelm her. The sculptural statement earrings and signature face-motif clutch brought just the right amount of the house’s eccentricity, while her slicked-back ponytail kept the overall look sharp and modern. The sculptural statement earrings and signature face-motif clutch brought just the right amount of the house’s eccentricity, while her slicked-back ponytail kept the overall look sharp and modern. item.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features
item.description: Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI As the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative. That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model . From Nigeria to Tanzania and Uganda, women across the continent are making their mark in pageantry, winning international titles, taking on national crowns and preparing to represent their countries on some of the world’s biggest stages. And there’s so much to know about the women behind these crowns. We’re talking about a medical doctor championing women’s health, a laboratory scientist making history internationally, and advocates using their platforms to support causes they care about. So if you love keeping up with the continent’s brightest trailblazers, these five reigning beauty queens definitely need to be on your radar. Osele Iruomachukwu: Miss Continental World 2026 Osele officially made history by claiming the inaugural title of Miss Continental World 2026 in Ayutthaya, Thailand. When she isn’t serving pure editorial elegance on international runways, she is busy putting her medical laboratory science degree and entrepreneurial background to work. Bringing home a major global win, she is representing Nigeria with serious pride and showing the world what true excellence looks like on the world stage. Osele Iruomachukwu after winning the inaugural Miss Continental World 2026 title in Thailand. Combining striking runway charm with a fierce passion for peace advocacy and global humanitarian work, Jihan has captured the hearts of audiences across multiple continents. Jihan Mohin Dimack celebrating her historic win as Miss Grand International 2026 in Bangkok, Thailand. Mitchelle Daka representing Uganda as Miss Universe Uganda 2026. item.title: Cardi B Makes Her Tiny Desk Debut With “Bodak Yellow,” “Be Careful” & More | Watch
item.description: Autographed polaroid photo of Cardi B at the NPR Music office for her Tiny Desk Concert set. Photo Credit: NPR Music/Instagram If you thought you knew what a Cardi B live set looked like, think again. The rap superstar recently stepped into the NPR Music office for her debut Tiny Desk Concert, and the atmosphere was nothing short of electric. Word got out fast, drawing one of the biggest crowds the office has ever seen as people from all walks of life lined up to watch hip-hop’s most unfiltered star take over the iconic workspace. Dressed sharply in leather trousers and a power blazer, Cardi brought a refreshingly humble and humorous spirit to the desk, delivering a masterclass in stage presence. Kicking things off with the haunting synths and outright confidence of “ Hello ,” she immediately set the tone before riding that unstoppable energy into a reimagined version of “ ErrTime .” Never one to shy away from versatility, she then shifted gears into deeply personal material, performing the vulnerable “ Man of Your Word ” and “ Be Careful ” while keeping her trademark wit and humor intact. “Change the vibes, change the vibes,” she joked with a smile, before bringing the ultimate party back with “ Up ,” which slid straight into “ AH HA .” To close out the unforgettable set, she treated the packed room to two pivotal anthems from her legendary catalogue: “ Bodak Yellow ,” the breakout hit that started it all, and the boogaloo-heavy crowd-pleaser “ I Like It .” By the end of the set, Cardi was swinging her hips right along with the ecstatic crowd, leaving the room beaming with gratitude and handing out warm hugs to a few lucky audience members. It is safe to say the Desk has never seen anything quite like it. Watch below The post Cardi B Makes Her Tiny Desk Debut With “Bodak Yellow,” “Be Careful” & More | Watch appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Meet Nkechi Okenwa, the Engineer Helping More Nigerian Women Break Into Renewable Energy
item.description: Tokunbo Adegoju during an interview with bird story agency at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency Nkechi Okenwa walked into her office, moving instinctively toward the window and pulled the blinds open. Outside, the city was already in motion: cars weaving through traffic, traders arranging their stalls, generators humming faintly in the distance. She paused for a moment and smiled quietly to herself. For Nkechi, energy had never simply been about electricity. It was about movement, opportunity, and the power to transform lives. Long before she stepped into a university lecture hall, Nkechi said, she had been fascinated by the way a single switch could completely change the atmosphere of a home. Growing up in Nigeria, she watched how electricity brought light into dark rooms and how access to power allowed communities and businesses to function. “As a teenager choosing the course of study, I had to take on electrical electronics engineering as a course,” she recalls. “Though I knew it was a male-dominated call, because I never saw any female studying that course… that’s actually how this whole journey started.” When she finally entered university, the reality of that gender gap became impossible to ignore. In a lecture hall of more than 220 engineering students, only 12 were women — barely five percent of the class. The imbalance was intimidating, but it also planted the seed for a bigger mission. Tokunbo Adegoju during her radio show at the Eko FM in LTV premises 1, lateef Jakande way , Agidingbi ikeja, Lagos, July 9, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency “I said there has to be a way to, you know, get women inclusive.” “I understand the challenges that come with a female being in this male-dominated industry, but when I look at myself and I can remember how I was able to go through, the challenges, my persistence, and all of that, I told myself it’s possible that so many other women too have aspirations to make a difference in their world and can also do this, so it made me start thinking of starting this organisation.” Years later, that determination evolved into two major ventures. Today, Nkechi serves as the CEO of Energy Excell Systems and Solutions and is also the founder of the Women in Energy and Economic Sustainability Initiative (WEESI), which is dedicated to integrating women into every level of the renewable energy sector. Tokunbo Adegoju repairing a car at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency Her professional journey did not begin with entrepreneurship. After graduating, she started as a technical staff member at an IT company where she worked with power systems and tools like AutoCAD. Through workshops, conferences, and industry engagements, she became increasingly exposed to the renewable energy sector at a time when Nigeria was slowly beginning to embrace alternative energy solutions. item.dc:creator: Bird
item.content:encoded: Tokunbo Adegoju during an interview with bird story agency at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency Nkechi Okenwa walked into her office, moving instinctively toward the window and pulled the blinds open. Outside, the city was already in motion: cars weaving through traffic, traders arranging their stalls, generators humming faintly in the distance. She paused for a moment and smiled quietly to herself. For Nkechi, energy had never simply been about electricity. It was about movement, opportunity, and the power to transform lives. Long before she stepped into a university lecture hall, Nkechi said, she had been fascinated by the way a single switch could completely change the atmosphere of a home. Growing up in Nigeria, she watched how electricity brought light into dark rooms and how access to power allowed communities and businesses to function. “As a teenager choosing the course of study, I had to take on electrical electronics engineering as a course,” she recalls. “Though I knew it was a male-dominated call, because I never saw any female studying that course… that’s actually how this whole journey started.” When she finally entered university, the reality of that gender gap became impossible to ignore. In a lecture hall of more than 220 engineering students, only 12 were women — barely five percent of the class. The imbalance was intimidating, but it also planted the seed for a bigger mission. Tokunbo Adegoju during her radio show at the Eko FM in LTV premises 1, lateef Jakande way , Agidingbi ikeja, Lagos, July 9, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency “I said there has to be a way to, you know, get women inclusive.” “I understand the challenges that come with a female being in this male-dominated industry, but when I look at myself and I can remember how I was able to go through, the challenges, my persistence, and all of that, I told myself it’s possible that so many other women too have aspirations to make a difference in their world and can also do this, so it made me start thinking of starting this organisation.” Years later, that determination evolved into two major ventures. Today, Nkechi serves as the CEO of Energy Excell Systems and Solutions and is also the founder of the Women in Energy and Economic Sustainability Initiative (WEESI), which is dedicated to integrating women into every level of the renewable energy sector. Tokunbo Adegoju repairing a car at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency Her professional journey did not begin with entrepreneurship. After graduating, she started as a technical staff member at an IT company where she worked with power systems and tools like AutoCAD. Through workshops, conferences, and industry engagements, she became increasingly exposed to the renewable energy sector at a time when Nigeria was slowly beginning to embrace alternative energy solutions. She later transitioned into a sales executive role before eventually building her own solar installation company. Established in 2013, Energy Excell Systems and Solutions Limited operates as an indigenous Nigerian renewable energy social enterprise and Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) company. But beyond simply installing solar panels, the company focused heavily on what Nkechi describes as “productive use” energy. The company provided homes, small businesses, and farming communities with energy-efficient appliances such as solar-powered rice mills, cassava graters, and grinders: tools capable of directly improving livelihoods and local economies. Tokunbo Adegoju and fellow mechanics discussing with each other at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency As her business expanded, Nkechi noticed another problem that extended far beyond electricity access. Women remained largely absent from conversations around energy solutions, despite being among the most affected by energy poverty within communities. “I looked at women, and I found that most challenges in the community that we face, we face them as men and women, but I find that women sometimes are not really included in solving these challenges, so I told myself I have to find a way to get women to across all levels.” That realisation led to the creation of WEESI in 2020. The initiative was designed to create pathways for women and girls across the energy value chain, from rural communities at the bottom of the energy pyramid to leadership spaces within the sector. The organisation strategically tailored its programs across different age groups. For girls and young women between the ages of 12 and 26, WEESI organised STEM essay competitions, mentorship programmes, and scholarship opportunities aimed at nurturing early interest in renewable energy and engineering. Tokunbo Adegoju and fellow mechanics discussing with each other at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency At the grassroots level, the initiative focused heavily on economic empowerment. Rural women, community entrepreneurs, and internally displaced persons (IDPs) received technical training in solar photovoltaic installation and maintenance while also learning sustainable clean cooking practices. “We have carried out programs and trainings with women in the rural areas, ranging from telling them how to turn the waste in the community into energy, like making and manufacturing charcoal briquettes with the waste in the community. For example, a woman that threshes rice and has a heap of rice husk doesn’t even know what to do with it. Now, can decarbonise this rice husk into charcoal and make briquettes with them, and make profitable money from it?” For many women, the impact of WEESI became life-changing. Tokunbo Adegoju and fellow mechanics discussing with each other at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency Among them was Anita Manuel , an entrepreneur and contractor working with an oil and gas firm. Anita first encountered WEESI during its launch and immediately felt drawn to the organisation’s mission. “What drew me to the initiative is that their objectives aligned with my values and goals too, and I just wanted to expand my business,” Manuel said. Through the training, Manuel learned practical skills in solar panel installation, energy auditing, and technical troubleshooting. More importantly, she began to see how her background in project management and civil works could fit into the renewable energy sector. One moment, however, remained unforgettable. The first time she participated in a successful solar installation that powered an entire building and activated a freezer became a defining experience. For Manuel, it was proof that the technical knowledge she had gained was not theoretical; it was transformative. Mechanics at the Automedics workshop repairing a car in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency For Nkechi, her growing influence in the renewable energy space was a quieter battle many women in STEM continue to face: self-doubt and institutional bias. Even after earning her engineering degree, she often questioned whether people would truly trust her expertise in such a male-dominated field. “My fears were, are you sure that I’m going to do it right? Are you sure people are going to listen to me because I’m a woman?” Those fears were reinforced repeatedly in professional spaces. Clients frequently walked into her office searching for a male engineer, assuming she could not possibly hold the technical expertise herself. Tokunbo Adegoju engaging with new students on their first day at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. item.title: Cynthia Erivo’s Fashion Range Is Beyond Impeccable
item.description: @jasonbolden If there’s one thing Cynthia Erivo has mastered, it’s the art of keeping us guessing. Whether she’s embracing full-throttle red carpet glamour or experimenting with more directional silhouettes, the British actress rarely plays it safe. And judging by her latest appearances, she’s showing no signs of slowing down. For the Prima Facie premiere at the BFI London Film Festival, Cynthia delivered a welcome dose of sunshine in a custom canary-yellow Prada gown. The bias-cut satin skimmed her figure beautifully, falling into a sweeping train, while oversized black grosgrain bows at the shoulders added a graphic contrast to the otherwise minimalist silhouette. @jasonbolden And she’s just as convincing in something that’s more casual but still directional. Case in point: the tan leather Proenza Schouler Fall 2026 co-ord she wore in New York. With its structured double-breasted jacket, relaxed trousers and chunky platform shoes, the look could easily have felt overwhelming. Instead, Cynthia made a compelling case for exaggerated proportions, proving that a neutral palette doesn’t have to mean playing it safe. Her final appearance at New York Comic Con, where she joined the cast of Children of Blood and Bone in another Proenza Schouler Fall 2026 creation also designed by new Proenza Schouler Creative Director Rachel Scott (also of Diotima). This time, she opted for a navy printed dress featuring sculptural draping, an asymmetric silhouette and dramatic fringed detailing. The silver grommets along the hem introduced an unexpected industrial edge, while glittering blue heels and statement jewellery completed the look. There were lots of moments like that. Continue reading...

item.title: See Inside Cells Like Never Before in These Vivid Microscopic Images
item.description: On a frigid February morning in Edinburgh, Scotland, Patrick Hickey had run out of living things to put under his microscope. The plants and fungi in his garden had dried up, and summer puddles, with their flamboyant biological complexity, had long frozen over. Hickey, a mycologist at Hypha Research Ltd., was using plant leaves to study mitochondria, cellular organelles that generate energy. Source

item.title: Manchester City have been a joy to watch but they became detached from their roots | Philipp Lahm
item.description: City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward Do we have to reassess Manchester City now? In my columns, I have repeatedly engaged with this club and its key figures. Looking back at what I have written over the years, I believe it remains beyond question that the team have achieved greatness. I always loved watching them: they were a true unit on the pitch, a finely tuned orchestra. I would also write all over again that the conductor, Pep Guardiola, masters his craft like few others. I could recognise his teams even if they were wearing the wrong shirts and the game was broadcast in black and white – by the passes, the distances between the players and the intelligence of their interplay. It is no wonder Guardiola inspires others to become managers; look at Vincent Kompany, Mikel Arteta, Enzo Maresca, and perhaps some time Ilkay Gündogan and Rodri. Continue reading...

Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way. Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further. Continue reading...

item.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
item.description: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal . That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...

item.title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked
item.description: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android Google’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out. For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/ $899 / A$2,299 ) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks. Continue reading...

item.title: Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: Diego Gómez’s wondergoal in a five-star demolition is just the latest in an impressive run of results for the south coast team Sign up for our free newsletter here For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes. This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League? Continue reading...

item.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
item.description: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago. Continue reading...

item.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
item.description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.” Continue reading...

I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.” Continue reading...

item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. Continue reading...

item.title: Mac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more pricey
item.description: Apple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouse Apple’s latest Mac mini brings real speed and power for far more than everyday tasks in a practically pocketable form you can fit almost anywhere. The impressive new desktop machine is the first to receive an update to Apple’s latest M6 chip while remaining smaller than a headphones box. It is the cheapest computer Apple sells with an M-series chip, but like every other memory-containing piece of electronics, it has been hit by RAMageddon , driving up the starting price to £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) from the £599 or equivalent of its M4 predecessor. item.title: Lunar Occultation of Venus
item.description: On Wednesday, June 17, skywatchers across the United States—and parts of Canada—enjoyed a rare event: a daytime lunar occultation of Venus. A lunar occultation occurs when the Moon moves directly in front of another celestial object from our viewpoint on Earth, briefly hiding it from sight.

item.title: August Lunar Eclipse Rises Over Louisiana
item.description: A lunar eclipse is visible over southern Louisiana. The lunar eclipse was visible throughout much of North and South America and part of Europe and Africa between Aug. 27-28. The Full Moon slipped through Earth’s shadow on Aug. 27, continuing into Aug. 28 for some parts of the world, resulting in the lunar eclipse. At maximum eclipse, the Moon takes on a dramatic dark, ruddy or coppery tint along the covered edge. New Orleans is home to NASA’s Michoud Assembly Facility, where stages for NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and structures for Orion spacecraft are produced for the Artemis missions.

item.title: Colorful Collage of Tarantula Nebula
item.description: Like a collage made of layered sheets of colored cellophane, a vibrant new image layers observations of a famous star-forming nebula from NASA space telescopes. The resulting cosmic “craft” reveals new details about the star formation region known as 30 Doradus, or the Tarantula Nebula.

item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game. Continue reading...
